cocktails.name: Amaretto Sour
cocktails.instructions: Combine all ingredients in a shaker and dry shake without ice to build the foam. Add ice and shake again until well chilled. Fine strain into a rocks glass over fresh ice. Garnish with a lemon twist and a brandied cherry.
cocktails.notes: The overproof bourbon is non-negotiable — it provides the backbone that makes this drink work. Without it, the amaretto overwhelms. Overproof means 100 proof (50% ABV) or higher; the higher the better. Morgenthaler recommends Bookers (typically 120-130 proof, uncut and unfiltered straight from the barrel), and he also recommends Old Grand-Dad 114 as an excellent, more accessible option. Any cask-strength bourbon in the 110-130 proof range will work beautifully. Dry shake first to build the foam, then shake with ice. Fine strain to keep it clean. Luxardo amaretto is also recommended.
cocktails.lore: In 2012, Jeffrey Morgenthaler published a post titled I Make the Best Amaretto Sour in the World. The craft cocktail world had spent a decade treating the Amaretto Sour as a punchline. Morgenthaler disagreed. His revamped version adds overproof bourbon for backbone and egg white for texture, transforming a drink everyone had written off into something genuinely elegant. It is now considered a modern classic and a defining moment of the cocktail revival — proof that rehabilitation is possible. Search Morgenthaler to find all three of his recipes in the collection.

cocktails.name: Americano
cocktails.instructions: Build in a highball glass over ice. Add Campari, then sweet vermouth, then soda. Stir gently. Garnish with an expressed orange peel.
cocktails.notes: The Americano is the lighter, lower-ABV cousin of the Negroni. It's the perfect aperitivo when you want something refreshing and bitter without the gin's punch. Adding gin to an Americano and removing the soda gives you a Negroni.
cocktails.lore: The Americano dates to 1860s Milan where it was called the Milano-Torino (Campari from Milan, vermouth from Turin). The name Americano came later — either because it was popular with American tourists, or in honor of boxer Primo Carnera. James Bond orders one in the very first chapter of Casino Royale before he upgrades to martinis. It is the direct parent of the Negroni — add gin and remove the soda.
cocktails.riffs: Negroni: add gin. Sbagliato: substitute Prosecco for soda water.

cocktails.name: Americano
cocktails.instructions: Build in a rocks glass over ice. Add Campari and sweet vermouth, then top with soda water. Stir gently. Garnish with an orange slice or lemon twist.
cocktails.notes: The Americano is the ancestor of the Negroni — substitute gin for the soda water and you have one. Lower-ABV, endlessly refreshing, and the perfect introduction to the bitter aperitivo style. James Bond orders one in the first chapter of Casino Royale — his very first drink in the entire canon.
cocktails.lore: The Americano traces directly to the Milano Torino — equal parts Campari and sweet vermouth — which had been popular in Italy since the 1860s. When American soldiers arrived in Italy during World War I, many found the Mi-To too bitter and too strong. Italian bartenders began adding soda water to lengthen and lighten it for their American guests. The name stuck. It is one of the oldest drinks in the Campari lineage and the direct precursor to the Negroni — Count Camillo Negroni simply asked his bartender to replace the soda with gin.
cocktails.riffs: Negroni: add gin. Sbagliato: substitute Prosecco for soda.

cocktails.name: Ancho Problem
cocktails.instructions: Combine all ingredients in a shaker with ice. Shake until well chilled. Fine strain into a chilled coupe or cocktail glass. No garnish needed.
cocktails.notes: Ancho Reyes and blanco tequila in equal parts is a bold structure — the chile liqueur is assertive and the tequila needs to match it. Use a bright, clean blanco with good agave presence rather than a softer, rounder style. Demerara syrup rather than simple syrup adds a molasses depth that rounds out the heat. The equal-parts build makes this easy to scale for batching.
cocktails.lore: Created by Ezra Star at Drink in Boston — a legendary menu-less bar where bartenders took requests and built drinks on the spot. The most common ask at Drink was something spicy with tequila, and the Ancho Problem was Star go-to answer. The name is self-aware: Ancho Reyes is both the solution to the request and, if you are not careful with the pour, the problem. A four-ingredient equal-parts build that does exactly what it promises — spicy, tequila, and nothing else to worry about.
cocktails.riffs: Substitute Ancho Reyes Verde for a greener, more herbaceous heat. Add a dash of mole bitters for additional complexity. A salted rim turns it toward Margarita territory.

cocktails.name: Aperol Spritz
cocktails.instructions: Build in a large wine glass over ice. Add Aperol first, then prosecco, then a splash of soda. Gently stir once. Garnish with a slice of orange or an expressed orange peel.
cocktails.notes: The 3-2-1 ratio (prosecco-Aperol-soda) is the classic formula. Some prefer 2-2-1 for a boozier version. Always build in the glass — never shake or stir aggressively or you'll lose the bubbles.
cocktails.lore: The Aperol Spritz follows the Venetian spritz tradition dating to the 19th century, when Austrian soldiers stationed in the Veneto diluted local wines with a spritz (splash) of water. Aperol itself was created in Padua in 1919. Though long popular in northern Italy, the drink became a global phenomenon after Campari Group's aggressive marketing campaign in the 2000s — making it the defining aperitivo of a generation.
cocktails.riffs: Campari Spritz: substitute Campari for a more bitter, less sweet result. Hugo Spritz: substitute elderflower liqueur and add mint.

cocktails.name: Army & Navy
cocktails.instructions: Combine all ingredients in a shaker with ice. Shake hard for 8-10 seconds. Fine strain into a chilled coupe. Garnish with a lemon peel or nothing at all.
cocktails.notes: Three ingredients. The quality of each matters enormously. A good London Dry with botanical complexity is the right choice — the orgeat needs a gin with something to say. Liber & Co. orgeat is the house recommendation. The original 2:1:1 recipe (equal parts gin, lemon, orgeat) is too sweet; the 8:2:1 Embury version is too dry. The balanced 8:3:2 ratio — 2oz gin, 3/4oz lemon, 1/2oz orgeat — is where this drink lives.
cocktails.lore: One of the great deep cuts of the classic cocktail canon, and one of the most underserved. First appears — as a name only, with no recipe — in William Tarling 1937 Cafe Royal Bar Book. The first actual recipe arrives in David Embury 1948 The Fine Art of Mixing Drinks, where Embury published the original 2:1:1 formula alongside his own withering assessment: I have given you the original recipe, which I think is horrible. Embury thinned it out considerably; subsequent bartenders found the middle ground. The drink may have originated at The Army and Navy Club in Washington D.C., the same officers club said to have introduced the Daiquiri to the United States. Nobody knows for certain, which is partly why it remains a deep cut rather than a household name. It deserves better.
cocktails.riffs: Mexico Navy: substitute blanco tequila for gin, lime for lemon, add ginger syrup. A dash of aromatic bitters adds structure without changing the character. Add a barspoon of amaretto alongside the orgeat for a richer, more dessert-forward version.

cocktails.name: Bee's Knees
cocktails.instructions: Make honey syrup by combining equal parts honey and warm water and stirring until dissolved. Combine gin, lemon juice, and honey syrup in a shaker with ice. Shake hard for 15 seconds. Double strain into a chilled coupe. Garnish with a lemon peel.
cocktails.notes: Make your honey syrup fresh — it keeps in the fridge for two weeks. The floral quality of honey pairs beautifully with botanical gins. Lavender honey gives a particularly lovely result.
cocktails.lore: The Bee's Knees was born during Prohibition in the 1920s, when honey and lemon were used to mask the rough taste of bathtub gin. The name was 1920s slang for the best of something — like the cat's pajamas. It is a gin sour with honey substituting for simple syrup, and represents the broader category of honey-sweetened cocktails that includes the Gold Rush (bourbon) and the Brown Derby (grapefruit).
cocktails.riffs: Substitute rye for gin for a spicier, more spirit-forward version. Add a barspoon of elderflower liqueur for a floral lift.

cocktails.name: Bellini
cocktails.instructions: Spoon white peach purée into a chilled champagne flute. Slowly top with prosecco, pouring down the side of the glass. Stir very gently once with a long spoon.
cocktails.notes: White peaches are essential — yellow peaches lack the delicacy. Fresh white peach purée in season is transcendent; good quality frozen purée works well year-round. Never use canned peaches.
cocktails.lore: The Bellini was created by Giuseppe Cipriani, founder of Harry's Bar in Venice, in 1948 and named after the Venetian Renaissance painter Giovanni Bellini whose works feature a particular shade of pink. It is made exclusively with white peach purée and Prosecco — the use of yellow peaches or champagne is considered a heresy by purists. Harry's Bar in Venice still serves the original, and it remains one of the most elegant and seasonally perfect cocktails ever conceived.
cocktails.riffs: Rossini: substitute strawberry puree for peach. Tintoretto: substitute pomegranate juice.

cocktails.name: Berry Gin Fizz
cocktails.instructions: Lightly muddle the berries in the glass. Add gin, lemon juice, simple syrup, and ice. Stir gently to combine. Top with soda water. Garnish with a mint sprig for extra freshness.
cocktails.notes: The recipe calls for The Great Eight Gin, an Austrian craft dry gin from the Peter Affenzeller distillery in Upper Austria, named for its eight botanicals. Any quality dry gin works beautifully. Use raspberries for tartness, blueberries for a deeper, earthier note, or a mix of both.
cocktails.lore: Discovered on a German cocktail website, this is a modern riff on the classic Gin Fizz — one of the most enduring cocktail families of the 1920s. The addition of fresh berries gives it a playful, summery character that feels entirely contemporary. The Fizz family template — spirit, citrus, sweetener, soda — is one of the most riff-able in the cocktail canon.

cocktails.name: Boulevardier
cocktails.instructions: Combine bourbon, Campari, and sweet vermouth in a mixing glass with ice. Stir for 30 seconds. Strain over a large ice cube in a rocks glass. Garnish with an expressed orange peel.
cocktails.notes: The Boulevardier is richer and softer than a Negroni — the bourbon's caramel and vanilla notes round out Campari's bitterness beautifully. Rye whiskey makes it spicier and drier.
cocktails.lore: The Boulevardier was created by Erskine Gwynne, an American expatriate who published a Paris magazine called The Boulevardier in the 1920s. It is a Negroni with bourbon replacing gin — same template, dramatically different character. While the Negroni was rediscovered in the 1990s cocktail renaissance, the Boulevardier languished until the bourbon boom of the 2010s brought it back to prominence.
cocktails.riffs: Old Pal: substitute dry vermouth for sweet. Rye Boulevardier: substitute rye for bourbon for a spicier result.

cocktails.name: Bourbon Renewal
cocktails.instructions: Shake all ingredients with ice until cold. Strain over fresh ice into a rocks glass. Garnish with a lemon wedge or fresh currants if in season.
cocktails.notes: Use a 1:1 simple syrup, not rich syrup — Morgenthaler confirmed this himself. The creme de cassis is the move; it adds berry depth without demanding attention. A lemon wedge garnish is sufficient but fresh currants in season are exceptional.
cocktails.lore: Created in 2001 at Bel Ami Lounge in Eugene, Oregon — before PDT, before Death & Co, before most of the craft cocktail revolution had a name. Jeffrey Morgenthaler named it after a band his business partner Tony Figoli had been in years before. He threw it on the Clyde Common menu when he moved to Portland, expecting to replace it. It became the bar best-selling drink by a wide margin — nearly 10,000 served per year. A Whiskey Sour punched up with creme de cassis and bitters, it sits somewhere between Dick Bradsell Bramble and the New York Sour, and is every bit as good as either. | Search Morgenthaler to find more of his recipes.
cocktails.riffs: Substitute rye for bourbon for a spicier, drier result.

cocktails.name: Brandy Alexander
cocktails.instructions: Combine cognac, crème de cacao, and cream in a shaker with ice. Shake hard for 20 seconds. Strain into a chilled coupe. Grate fresh nutmeg over the top.
cocktails.notes: Fresh nutmeg grated over the top is essential — pre-ground nutmeg is a poor substitute. Use dark crème de cacao for a richer chocolate flavor. This is a dessert cocktail — rich, sweet, and deeply satisfying.
cocktails.lore: The Alexander cocktail appeared in print as early as 1915, originally made with gin. The Brandy Alexander — substituting cognac for gin — became the dominant version and a symbol of 1970s cocktail glamour. John Lennon was famously photographed drinking one at the beginning of his Lost Weekend period in Los Angeles. It belongs to the Flip and Cream family, alongside the Grasshopper and Pink Squirrel.
cocktails.riffs: Add a barspoon of orange liqueur for a more citrus-forward result. Substitute aged rum for brandy for a Caribbean variation.

cocktails.name: Brandy Crusta
cocktails.instructions: Prepare the glass first: moisten the rim of a coupe with a lemon wedge and dip in fine sugar to create the crusta. Peel a long spiral of lemon peel and place it inside the glass so it lines the interior — this is the defining presentation. Combine cognac, Cointreau, lemon juice, maraschino, and bitters in a shaker with ice. Shake until well chilled. Strain carefully into the prepared glass.
cocktails.notes: The long spiral lemon peel lining the glass interior is not optional — it is the crusta that names the drink. The presentation is the point. Take time with it. Fine sugar gives a more elegant crust than coarse. The drink is quite dry; the sugar rim and maraschino provide the only sweetness.
cocktails.lore: Created by Joseph Santini at the City Exchange bar in New Orleans around 1850 — making it one of the oldest identifiable cocktail recipes in American history. The Brandy Crusta is the missing link between the Fancy Cocktail of the 1840s and the Sidecar of the 1920s. It introduced the sugar-rimmed glass and the citrus peel lining — both of which became defining elements of classic cocktail presentation. Without the Brandy Crusta there is no Sidecar, and without the Sidecar there is arguably no Daisy family. Jerry Thomas included it in his 1862 How to Mix Drinks, cementing its place in the canon. It fell out of fashion for over a century before the craft cocktail revival restored it to its proper place: at the beginning of everything.
cocktails.riffs: The Sidecar is a direct descendant — Cointreau, lemon, cognac, no bitters, no maraschino, no crusta. Compare the two side by side for a lesson in how a template evolves.

cocktails.name: Caipirinha
cocktails.instructions: Cut off the top and tail of the lime half and remove the white pith from the center. Cut into 4 wedges and add to a sturdy rocks glass with the sugar. Muddle firmly, pressing on the flesh rather than the skin to avoid bitterness. Add cachaca and fill with ice. Stir until well chilled, about 20 seconds. No garnish needed — the lime is already in the glass.
cocktails.notes: The white pith is the enemy — remove it before muddling or it will add bitterness. Press on the flesh, not the skin. Brazilian tradition says stirred, never shaken. Use 2 teaspoons of sugar as a starting point and adjust to your lime and preference. Leblon and Novo Fogo are excellent cachacas for the Caipirinha.
cocktails.lore: The national cocktail of Brazil and one of the great three-ingredient drinks in the world. Cachaca, lime, sugar — that is all. The name means little country girl in Portuguese, and the drink most likely originated in Sao Paulo, though its precise history is contested. One persistent theory holds that an early version was created as a folk remedy during the Spanish Flu pandemic of 1918 — cachaca, lime, honey, and garlic — and that the garlic was eventually dropped as the drink moved from medicine cabinet to bar. In 2003 the Brazilian government officially declared it the national cocktail. In 2024 it ranked third in the world on TasteAtlas. Cachaca is not rum — both come from sugarcane, but cachaca is distilled from fresh-pressed cane juice while rum is made from molasses. That difference is everything.
cocktails.riffs: Strawberry Caipirinha: muddle 3-4 hulled strawberries with the lime and sugar before adding cachaca. Passionfruit Caipirinha: add 1 oz fresh passionfruit pulp. Caipiroska: substitute vodka for cachaca. Caipirissima: substitute white rum for cachaca.

cocktails.name: Cantaloupe and Fresno Chile Spritzer
cocktails.instructions: Process cantaloupe and Fresno chile in a food processor until smooth, about 1 minute, scraping down as needed. Strain through a fine-mesh strainer into a pitcher. Just before serving, gently stir in chilled seltzer. Pour into ice-filled glasses. For a single portion, use 1/4 cup puree and 3/4 cup seltzer, then add ice.
cocktails.notes: The puree can be refrigerated up to 2 days. This is intentionally austere: ripe melon, fresh chile heat, and bubbles. Use good cantaloupe or the drink has nowhere to hide.
cocktails.lore: Created by Hannah Fenton for America's Test Kitchen (November 2022). The recipe is almost audaciously simple — three ingredients — but the Fresno chile gives ripe cantaloupe enough tension to read like a composed zero-proof cocktail.
cocktails.riffs: Try basil or mint as an aromatic garnish. For more heat, let the chile sit briefly in the strained puree before adding seltzer, then strain again.

cocktails.name: Carajillo
cocktails.instructions: Pull a fresh shot of espresso. Fill a Nick & Nora or rocks glass with ice. Pour Licor 43 over the ice first. Slowly pour the hot espresso over the back of a spoon to create a layered effect — the hot espresso will float briefly before integrating. Serve immediately.
cocktails.notes: The layered pour is essential to the visual drama — hot espresso floating on cold Licor 43 is one of the most beautiful sights in cocktail making. Drink quickly to enjoy the temperature contrast. A double shot of espresso makes it more intense.
cocktails.lore: The Carajillo is a traditional Spanish and Latin American coffee drink with roots in the Cuban wars of independence, when Spanish soldiers allegedly mixed coffee with rum for courage — 'coraje' meaning courage. The modern Mexican version, made with Licor 43, became a phenomenon in upscale Mexico City bars in the 2010s before spreading globally. Licor 43 — a Spanish liqueur made from 43 ingredients including vanilla and citrus — was purpose-built for exactly this kind of combination.
cocktails.riffs: Substitute mezcal for espresso liqueur for a smokier, more Mexican-influenced variation.

cocktails.name: Champagne Cocktail
cocktails.instructions: Soak a sugar cube with Angostura bitters and drop it into the bottom of a chilled champagne flute. Add cognac. Top slowly with champagne. Garnish with a lemon peel.
cocktails.notes: Watch the sugar cube effervesce — it creates a constant stream of champagne bubbles that is one of the most beautiful sights in cocktail making. The cognac is traditional but optional.
cocktails.lore: The Champagne Cocktail is one of the oldest known cocktails, appearing in Jerry Thomas's 1862 bartending guide. It is elegant in its simplicity — a bitters-soaked sugar cube dropped into champagne creates both flavor and the mesmerizing spectacle of constant carbonation. It was the drink of choice at Truman Capote's legendary Black and White Ball at the Plaza Hotel in 1966, one of the most glamorous parties of the 20th century.
cocktails.riffs: Add a barspoon of cognac for a richer, more complex result. Substitute Angostura for Peychauds bitters for a New Orleans variation.

cocktails.name: Chestnut Cup
cocktails.instructions: Combine all ingredients in a shaker with a single ice cube. Shake to combine and chill without over-diluting. Strain into a Collins or rocks glass filled three-quarters with ice cubes. Top with crushed ice. Garnish with an orange slice or lemon wheel.
cocktails.notes: The single ice cube technique is deliberate — it chills and combines the drink without the full dilution of a full shake. The orgeat bridges the bitter Campari and bright lemon beautifully; do not skip it or substitute simple syrup. A botanical gin works particularly well here. House-made orgeat makes a noticeable difference.
cocktails.lore: Created at the Chestnut Club in Santa Monica, California. The drink sits at a fascinating intersection — it has the citrus-sweetener backbone of a Sour, the bitter complexity of a Campari build, and the nutty richness of a Tiki-adjacent orgeat ingredient, all in one glass. It should not work as well as it does. The name has nothing to do with chestnuts — it comes from the bar that made it, whose name comes from the street it sits on.
cocktails.riffs: Substitute Aperol for Campari for a softer, less bitter version. Gran Classico Bitter gives a more herbal, complex result. Add a dash of Angostura bitters for extra depth.

cocktails.name: Classic Daiquiri
cocktails.instructions: Combine all ingredients in a shaker with ice. Shake hard for 15 seconds. Double strain into a chilled coupe.
cocktails.notes: The Daiquiri is a bartender's benchmark — deceptively simple, ruthlessly revealing of technique and ingredient quality. Use fresh lime juice only. The ratio of sweet to sour is the whole game — taste and adjust before shaking.
cocktails.lore: The Daiquiri was born in the mining town of Daiquirí, Cuba around 1900, popularized by American engineer Jennings Cox. It belongs to the Sour family — spirit, citrus, sweetener — and is considered the purist's test of a bartender's skill. Hemingway famously drank them by the pitcher at El Floridita in Havana, though he requested his without sugar — the Papa Doble.
cocktails.riffs: Hemingway Daiquiri: add grapefruit juice and maraschino, no sugar. Banana Daiquiri: add banana liqueur. Strawberry Daiquiri: blend with fresh strawberries.

cocktails.name: Classic Margarita
cocktails.instructions: Prepare a margarita glass with a salted rim. Add tequila, Cointreau, lime juice, and agave syrup to a shaker tin. Add ice and shake hard for 15 seconds. Strain over fresh ice into the prepared glass. Garnish with a lime wheel.
cocktails.notes: Use the best blanco tequila you can — it makes an enormous difference. Agave syrup at 1:1 (agave:water) keeps the sweetness clean and true to the spirit.
cocktails.lore: The Margarita is technically a Daisy — a sour cocktail made with a base spirit, citrus, and an orange liqueur, served in a salt-rimmed glass. In fact, margarita is Spanish for daisy. It belongs to the same family as the Sidecar and Cosmopolitan, and is one of the most ordered cocktails in the world. Its precise origin is disputed, with several bartenders and socialites from the 1930s-50s claiming credit.
cocktails.riffs: Tommy Margarita: agave nectar instead of triple sec, on the rocks. Mezcal Margarita: substitute mezcal for tequila for a smoky version. Spicy Margarita: add jalapeno-infused tequila or muddle fresh chile.

cocktails.name: Classic Martini
cocktails.instructions: Stir gin, vermouth, and bitters with ice for 30-40 seconds until well chilled and properly diluted. Strain into a chilled martini or coupe glass. Express a lemon peel over the surface and either drop it in or perch it on the rim.
cocktails.notes: The ratio is everything — 5:1 is bone dry, 3:1 is classic, 2:1 is a wet martini. Chill your glass in the freezer. Never shake unless specifically asked — it bruises the gin and clouds the drink.
cocktails.lore: The Martini is arguably the most iconic cocktail in existence, its origins disputed between New York and San Francisco in the 1880s. It belongs to no family — it IS a family, the template from which the Manhattan, the Negroni, and countless others descend. Churchill famously chilled his gin by glancing at the vermouth bottle. James Bond's insistence on shaking it is, to purists, a cardinal sin.
cocktails.riffs: Gibson: substitute a cocktail onion garnish for the olive. Dirty Martini: add a barspoon of olive brine. Vesper: add 0.5 oz Lillet Blanc and substitute vodka for half the gin.

cocktails.name: Clover Club
cocktails.instructions: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice. Shake until well chilled and strain back into the empty tin. Shake again without ice — the reverse dry shake — until the foam builds. Pour into a chilled coupe. Garnish with 2-3 fresh raspberries on a skewer. For raspberry syrup: smash half cup fresh raspberries with 1 cup sugar and macerate for 30 minutes. Heat half cup water to warm (not hot) and pour over the fruit mixture. Stir until sugar dissolves. Strain through a chinois and fortify with half oz vodka to extend shelf life. The key is warm water not hot — hot water cooks the berries and produces a jam flavor rather than a bright fresh raspberry.
cocktails.notes: The reverse dry shake — shaking with ice first, then straining and shaking again without ice — produces a notably frothier, more stable foam than the standard dry shake first method. Julie Reiner calls it optional but it is worth doing. The dry vermouth is the critical addition: it adds dryness and complexity and is in fact the historically accurate spec, confirmed by food historian David Wondrich who found the original 1890s recipe with vermouth intact. Plymouth gin is recommended for its softer, less juniper-forward botanical profile.
cocktails.lore: Named for a Philadelphia men's literary club that met at the Bellevue-Stratford Hotel in the 1890s — the Clover Club cocktail predates Prohibition by two decades. The recipe that survived into the modern era had lost its dry vermouth somewhere along the way, making it sweeter and less complex than the original. Julie Reiner, who named her Brooklyn bar after the drink, restored the vermouth after historian David Wondrich found the original recipe in print. He apparently came running. The addition makes it more sophisticated and, it turns out, more historically accurate. Her bar has been making it this way since 2008. Even now, she notes with some amusement, you would think that more people would look to us for what the recipe should be.
cocktails.riffs: The quick version: substitute half oz simple syrup for the raspberry syrup and muddle 3-4 fresh raspberries directly in the shaker. Less concentrated but faster. The Rattlesnake is a close cousin in the egg white sour family.

cocktails.name: Coffee Cocktail
cocktails.instructions: Combine all ingredients in a shaker. Dry shake vigorously without ice for 10 seconds to emulsify. Add ice and shake hard until well chilled. Fine strain into a chilled wine glass or coupe. Grate fresh nutmeg generously over the surface.
cocktails.notes: Essentially a Porto Flip with cognac in place of brandy — the distinction is subtle but cognac adds a more refined aromatic quality. The drink looks like black coffee in the glass, which is the entire point of the name. Jerry Thomas himself noted the drink contains neither coffee nor bitters despite being called a cocktail, which in 1887 specifically implied the presence of bitters.
cocktails.lore: The best cocktail in the world named after what it is not. It contains no coffee. It barely qualifies as a cocktail by the 1887 definition — Jerry Thomas himself pointed this out in the recipe note: the name of this drink is a misnomer, as coffee and bitters are not to be found among its ingredients, but it looks like coffee when properly concocted, and hence its name. The appearance is the whole joke. Cognac and ruby port, whole egg, simple syrup — shaken until it is the color of cold espresso in a coupe glass. The nutmeg is the only garnish it needs.
cocktails.riffs: Use aged rum in place of cognac for a more tropical character. A barspoon of coffee liqueur leans into the name without actually being a Coffee Cocktail anymore.

cocktails.name: Cold Fashioned
cocktails.instructions: Add all ingredients to a blender and blend until smooth. Serve in a rocks glass. Garnish with a brulee sugar crisp. For the Old Fashioned mix: combine 150ml black tea, 150g sugar, and 14 dashes aromatic bitters. Stir until sugar dissolves. For the citrus blend: combine 2 parts fresh lemon juice, 1 part fresh orange juice, 1 part fresh grapefruit juice. For the brulee sugar crisp: cut the end off an orange and place it upside down on a jigger. Spread 1 barspoon sugar over the center, add 8-10 drops aromatic bitters, then caramelize with a kitchen torch until fully browned and bubbling. Add a pinch of flaky sea salt as it cools.
cocktails.notes: Xanthan gum is optional but recommended for texture — it prevents the blend from separating and gives the drink a smoother, more uniform consistency. A small amount goes a long way. Pre-made old fashioned mix and sour mix can substitute for the house-made versions but the scratch version is dramatically better. The brulee sugar crisp can be made ahead and stored briefly.
cocktails.lore: A house cocktail from Still Austin Whiskey Co., the first whiskey distillery in Austin city limits since Prohibition. Still Austin is a grain-to-glass operation — milling, mashing, fermenting, distilling, barreling, and bottling entirely in-house — and The Musician bourbon, their flagship, is what the drink is built around. The Cold Fashioned is served at their distillery bar on the east side of Austin, alongside tours, live music, and a seafood food truck on the patio. The recipe was popularized online by Austin-based mixologist Reid Nelson (@reidbetweenthelimes), who recreated the Still Austin version at home with characteristic attention to technique and garnish detail. The brulee sugar crisp is the signature detail: sugar, aromatic bitters, and flaky sea salt caramelized on an orange slice with a kitchen torch. The xanthan gum note is worth heeding — a quarter teaspoon is the difference between a smooth frozen cocktail and a separated one.
cocktails.riffs: Scale down to a single serving: 1.5oz bourbon, 0.75oz old fashioned mix, 2oz citrus blend, small pinch of xanthan gum, 4oz pebble ice. Substitute rye for a spicier result.

cocktails.name: Corpse Reviver No. 2
cocktails.instructions: Rinse a chilled coupe with absinthe — add a small amount, swirl to coat, and discard the excess. Combine gin, Cointreau, Lillet Blanc, and lemon juice in a shaker with ice. Shake well and strain into the prepared coupe. No garnish needed.
cocktails.notes: Equal parts is the classic spec and the right one. Lillet Blanc is the standard but Cocchi Americano gives a more bitter, quinine-forward result that some prefer — it is closer to the original Kina Lillet, which is no longer produced. The absinthe rinse is not optional; it perfumes every sip from the nose and gives the drink its distinctive anise undercurrent. Plymouth or a classic London Dry both work beautifully here.
cocktails.lore: Harry Craddock, head bartender at the American Bar at the Savoy Hotel in London, published this in The Savoy Cocktail Book in 1930 alongside the only instruction anyone remembers: Four of these taken in swift succession will unrevive the corpse again. The drink belongs to a family of cocktails called Corpse Revivers, originally intended as hair-of-the-dog hangover remedies — a tradition documented as far back as 1861 in Punch magazine. The No. 2 overtook every other version in the canon and never looked back. It is one of the great equal-parts cocktails: gin, Cointreau, Lillet, lemon, each pulling equal weight, with the absinthe rinse adding a fifth voice from the glass itself.
cocktails.riffs: Substitute Cocchi Americano for Lillet Blanc for a more bitter, historically accurate version. The Corpse Reviver No. 1 — brandy, apple brandy, sweet vermouth — is a stirred Manhattan-style drink that bears almost no resemblance to its famous sibling.

cocktails.name: Cosmopolitan
cocktails.instructions: Combine all ingredients in a shaker with ice. Shake hard for 15 seconds. Strain into a chilled martini glass. Garnish with an expressed orange peel.
cocktails.notes: Use just enough cranberry juice to give the drink its signature blush — more than half an ounce and it tips too sweet. Citrus vodka is traditional but a clean neutral vodka works equally well.
cocktails.lore: The Cosmopolitan was popularized by bartender Toby Cecchini at The Odeon in New York in 1988, though earlier versions existed in Florida and Provincetown. It became a cultural phenomenon through Sex and the City in the late 1990s, making it one of the most recognizable cocktails in the world. Technically a Daisy — spirit, citrus, orange liqueur — it shares its DNA with the Margarita and Sidecar.
cocktails.riffs: Add a float of Cointreau for extra orange richness. Substitute blood orange juice for regular cranberry for a seasonal variation.

cocktails.name: Dame Blanche au Poire
cocktails.instructions: Place the gin, pear liqueur, and lemon juice in a cocktail shaker. Cover with ice and shake vigorously until well-chilled, about 15 seconds. Strain into a chilled coupe or small tulip glass. Garnish with a citrus peel.
cocktails.notes: Recipe by @bridget7487049 via ReciMe. Citadelle gin is recommended but any quality London Dry works well.
cocktails.lore: The Dame Blanche is a classic gin sour from the golden age of cocktails, named after the Belgian legend of a white-robed spirit said to haunt mountain passes. Structurally it belongs to the Sour family — spirit, citrus, sweetener — here elevated with pear liqueur for a delicate floral character.

cocktails.name: Dangerous Passion
cocktails.instructions: Combine the tequila, ginger liqueur, Ancho Reyes, and passion fruit juice in a shaker over ice. Shake vigorously for 30 seconds. Strain into a rocks glass over fresh ice. To garnish, lightly torch or briefly flame the dehydrated lime slice, the halved habanero pepper, and a pinch of cardamom seeds to release their aromas. Place on the rim or float on top of the drink.
cocktails.notes: The flamed garnish is essential to the experience — the scorched habanero and toasted cardamom transform the aromatic profile entirely. Fresh passion fruit juice is strongly preferred; bottled works but loses the floral brightness. Teremana Reposado brings a gentle oak and vanilla quality that bridges the fruit and heat beautifully.
cocktails.lore: Created at a beachside bar in Aruba, the Dangerous Passion — El Azarosa Passionato in its original Spanish-Italian — is a masterclass in the seductive tension between tropical sweetness and slow-building heat. The passion fruit opens bright and floral, the ginger adds warmth, and the Ancho Reyes delivers a long, smoky chile finish. The flamed garnish is theatre as much as technique — the scorched habanero releases capsaicin aromatics that prime the palate before the first sip. A cocktail that lives up to its name.
cocktails.riffs: Substitute gin for vodka for a more botanical version. Add a barspoon of grenadine for a deeper, richer color.

cocktails.name: Dark & Stormy
cocktails.instructions: Fill a highball glass with ice. Add lime juice. Pour ginger beer over the ice. Float dark rum on top by pouring it slowly over the back of a spoon. Garnish with a lime wheel. Stir gently before drinking.
cocktails.notes: Gosling's Black Seal is the traditional rum and actually holds a trademark on the name Dark 'n' Stormy with their rum. The float is visual drama — stir before drinking for the full flavor. Goslings or Plantation Original Dark both work beautifully.
cocktails.lore: The Dark & Stormy is the national drink of Bermuda, where Gosling's rum has been produced since 1806. It belongs to the Highball family alongside the Moscow Mule, and shares the same basic template — spirit, ginger beer, citrus. Gosling's Brothers trademarked the name Dark 'n' Stormy in the United States, making it the only cocktail with a legally protected recipe. The name evokes the color of the drink — dark rum floating above golden ginger beer.
cocktails.riffs: Moscow Mule: substitute vodka for rum. Use a smoky dark rum like Goslings for the most traditional version.

cocktails.name: Death Flip
cocktails.instructions: Combine all ingredients in a shaker. Dry shake vigorously without ice to emulsify the egg. Add ice and shake hard until well chilled. Fine strain into a chilled coupe. Grate fresh nutmeg over the surface.
cocktails.notes: The original spec used Herradura Blanco — the only widely available 100% agave tequila in Melbourne in 2010. Any quality blanco tequila works. Hysted-Adams later replaced the vanilla syrup with simple syrup to let the base spirits shine; both versions are excellent. Dry shake first — the egg needs to emulsify before dilution. The result is lighter and airier than expected. Reminiscent of spiced gingerbread eggnog.
cocktails.lore: Created in 2010 by Chris Hysted-Adams at the Black Pearl bar in Fitzroy, Melbourne — the only flip to become a modern classic. When it first appeared on the menu, no ingredients were listed. If you asked what was in it, the bartender would not tell you. The only description offered was: 'You don't wanna meet this cocktail in a dark alley.' Plenty of people took the dare, and many ended up liking it — something that almost certainly would not have happened if the ingredients had been listed upfront. Tequila, Yellow Chartreuse, Jagermeister, and a whole egg. The name is a reference to an acrobatic skateboard trick — daring, unexpected, and lands better than it has any right to.
cocktails.riffs: The original recipe called for a dash of vanilla syrup instead of simple syrup — try it both ways. A dash of Angostura adds structure.

cocktails.name: Distant Lover
cocktails.instructions: Combine all ingredients in a shaker with ice and shake until well chilled. Double strain into a rocks glass over a large ice cube. Garnish with a dehydrated citrus wheel or a small decorative heart pinned to the glass.
cocktails.notes: Amaro Sfumato Rabarbaro appears twice in this collection — here and in Thou Shall Not Be Named. It is a smoky rhubarb-root amaro from Cappelletti that is genuinely irreplaceable; do not substitute. For the strawberry syrup: simmer 600ml water with 150g sliced strawberries on low for 5 minutes. Strain the solids, then combine the liquid with an equal weight of sugar. Keeps refrigerated for 1 week. Double straining is essential here — the strawberry syrup can leave sediment.
cocktails.lore: Created by Mel Tate at Dovetail, named after the 1974 Marvin Gaye classic from Let Us Get It On. The name is earned: this is a summer sour with unexpected depth, built around the classic flavor combination of strawberry and rhubarb — but channeled through amaro and orgeat rather than a pie. Tate was named one of PUNCH best new bartenders in 2025. The decorative heart garnish is a small and perfect touch — the kind of detail that makes a drink feel like it was made for someone specific.
cocktails.riffs: Substitute mezcal for tequila for a smokier, more brooding version that leans further into the Sfumato character.

cocktails.name: Dove Dispatch
cocktails.instructions: Combine tequila, Campari, grapefruit juice, and bell pepper syrup in a shaker with ice. Shake and strain over ice into a Collins glass rimmed with chile salt. Top with soda water. No additional garnish needed — the chile salt rim is the garnish. For red bell pepper simple syrup: blend 1 chopped de-seeded red bell pepper with 8 oz water and 3/4 cup sugar on low for 30 seconds. Let sit overnight then strain out solids.
cocktails.notes: The bell pepper syrup is not negotiable — it is what makes this drink structurally distinct from a Paloma. Make it the day before and strain well. The chile salt rim adds heat that plays beautifully against the bitterness of the Campari. Any quality blanco tequila works; the vegetal agave note is in dialogue with the bell pepper.
cocktails.lore: Created by Meaghan Dorman at Dear Irving in New York City, one of the most celebrated cocktail bars in Manhattan. The brief was strong and savory — Dorman went for green and vegetal, combining Campari and tequila with fresh grapefruit and a housemade red bell pepper syrup that adds earthiness and body. The chile salt rim completes the picture. Described by Dorman as a drink where green, vegetal flavors combined with a hint of spice should still be bright and enjoyable, but with that extra subtle layer. First published in PUNCH in 2014 and has remained one of the most referenced savory tequila cocktails in the modern canon.
cocktails.riffs: Substitute mezcal for half the tequila for a smoky version. Yellow bell pepper syrup gives a slightly sweeter, milder result.

cocktails.name: First Class Pass
cocktails.instructions: Add cucumber slices and mint leaves to a shaker and muddle gently — bruise the cucumber and press the mint just enough to release the oils without shredding. Add Irish whiskey, elderflower liqueur, vodka, honey syrup, and lime juice. Add ice and shake well. Double strain through a fine strainer into an ice-filled highball glass. Top with chilled yuzu soda. Garnish with a lime wheel and mint sprig.
cocktails.notes: Fever-Tree Lime and Yuzu is the house soda at The Irish Exit — it is worth tracking down. In a pinch, any yuzu-forward soda or a combination of yuzu juice and plain soda water will work. Double strain to remove mint fragments and cucumber seeds. The small amounts of vodka and lime are balancers rather than primary flavors — do not skip them. Honey syrup is 1:1 honey to warm water, stirred until dissolved.
cocktails.lore: An evolution of an original recipe by Jack McGarry, managing partner of The Irish Exit in New York City — the sister bar to The Dead Rabbit, one of the most celebrated cocktail bars in the world. The drink matches cucumber and mint against the floral, herbal character of Irish whiskey, a pairing so natural it is surprising it is not more common. The elderflower liqueur ties both together. The yuzu soda adds a citrus brightness that keeps the whole thing from becoming heavy despite the multiple flavor elements at play.
cocktails.riffs: Substitute gin for Irish whiskey for a more botanical result. Add a barspoon of St-Germain in place of the elderflower liqueur for a slightly richer floral note.

cocktails.name: French 007
cocktails.instructions: Add the pear and pomegranate liqueurs to a chilled champagne flute. Top with dry champagne or sparkling wine. No stirring needed — the bubbles will do the work.
cocktails.notes: The Mathilde Poire and Pama create a beautiful rose-gold color in the glass. Use a genuinely dry champagne or crémant to keep it from tipping too sweet.
cocktails.lore: The French 007 is a champagne cocktail in the Kir Royale tradition — a style dating to post-war Burgundy, where Canon Félix Kir popularized the combination of crème de cassis and white wine. By substituting fruit liqueurs for cassis and using champagne, the format becomes endlessly riffable. The name nods to its Franco-elegant character — shaken, not stirred optional.
cocktails.riffs: Substitute rye for bourbon for a spicier, drier result. Add a barspoon of honey syrup for a Gold Rush variation.

cocktails.name: French 75
cocktails.instructions: Combine gin, lemon juice, and simple syrup in a shaker with ice. Shake for 10 seconds. Strain into a chilled champagne flute. Top with champagne. Garnish with a lemon peel.
cocktails.notes: Cognac is the traditional base in France; gin is the Anglo-American version. Either works beautifully. Use a genuinely dry champagne or crémant — the drink has enough sweetness already.
cocktails.lore: The French 75 was created at Harry's New York Bar in Paris in 1915, named after the French 75mm field gun because its kick was said to feel like being shelled by one. It belongs to the Fizz family — spirit, citrus, sweetener, topped with bubbles — and is one of the few truly great champagne cocktails. It was famously featured in the film Casablanca.
cocktails.riffs: Substitute rye for gin for a spicier, spirit-forward variation. Add a barspoon of St-Germain for a floral lift.

cocktails.name: French Blonde
cocktails.instructions: Combine all ingredients in a shaker with ice. Shake vigorously for 30 seconds. Double strain into a chilled coupe or Nick and Nora glass. Garnish with a grapefruit twist.
cocktails.notes: Use fresh grapefruit juice — not bottled. Oro Blanco (white grapefruit) gives the palest, most elegant color. Pink grapefruit works just as well and adds a peachy hue. A London dry gin is traditional but a citrus-forward gin elevates the floral notes beautifully.
cocktails.lore: The French Blonde is gin, Lillet Blanc, fresh grapefruit, and St-Germain elderflower — a drink that sits somewhere between a Greyhound and a White Negroni, floral and citrus-bright and unmistakably French in character. It came to widespread attention when US Weekly reported it as Taylor Swift favorite cocktail during the Eras Tour era — and if the Eras Tour can boost the global economy, a Swift endorsement was always going to move bottles of Lillet. Bartenders everywhere had better know how to make it. The good news: it deserves the attention entirely on its own merits.

cocktails.name: Fresh Fruit Citronade
cocktails.instructions: Muddle the strawberries, basil, simple syrup, and black pepper in a shaker until the berries are smashed and the basil is fragrant. Add the vodka, Solerno, lemon juice, and ice and shake vigorously for 10 seconds. Dirty pour the entire contents directly into a tall Collins glass. Top with a splash of soda water and garnish with a strawberry slice or fresh basil sprig.
cocktails.notes: The dirty pour keeps the muddled fruit in the glass, creating layered flavor as you drink. The black pepper is the secret — do not skip it. Solerno bridges the citrus and strawberry beautifully; Cointreau works as a substitute.
cocktails.lore: Started life as an Applebee's menu item — proof that chain restaurants occasionally stumble onto something worth stealing. Re-specced for Alchemy with fresh lemon, Solerno, and an extra crack of pepper. A dirty pour keeps the muddled fruit and broken ice in the glass, layering the flavor from first sip to last. Sorry, Applebee's.
cocktails.riffs: The original Applebee's spec that started this: 1.5 oz citron vodka, 2 fresh strawberries, 3 basil leaves, pinch of black pepper, good quality lemonade, seltzer. Build in glass — muddle strawberries, pepper, and basil gently, add vodka and ice and stir, top with lemonade and seltzer, then gently lift and stir to combine. The current Alchemy spec is a proper cocktail rebuild of that same spirit.

cocktails.name: Gargoyle
cocktails.instructions: If using fresh passion fruit, scoop out the interior, push through a fine strainer to remove seeds, and add an equal volume of simple syrup to sweeten. Add all ingredients including the lemon wheel to a shaker. Shake hard until well chilled. Strain into a pre-chilled coupe. Garnish with a lemon twist.
cocktails.notes: The lemon wheel goes into the shaker — it is muddled by the shaking process and contributes citrus oil and juice to the drink. Commercially available passion fruit puree works well here; if sweetened, use as-is. The equal-parts gin and vodka split is unusual — the vodka dilutes the gin botanicals and lets the passion fruit lead. A clean London Dry is the right gin choice.
cocktails.lore: Invented by George White, head bartender at the Gargoyle Club in Soho, London, and published in William Tarling 1937 Cafe Royal Cocktail Book — attributed simply to G. White. Tarling, who also published the first known Toreador and Army and Navy recipes, made a habit of preserving the work of London barmen who might otherwise have vanished from history entirely. The Gargoyle Club itself was founded in 1925 by aristocrat David Tennant and occupied a Soho townhouse designed in part by Henri Matisse. By day it served business lunches. By night it became something else entirely. Among its members: Guy Burgess, Donald MacLean, and Kim Philby — three of the Cambridge Five, the most consequential spy ring in British history. They drank here. They schemed here. They ordered this cocktail, or something like it, while passing secrets to Moscow. The Gargoyle is a three-ingredient equal-parts drink — gin, vodka, passion fruit — deceptively simple for a venue that was anything but.
cocktails.riffs: Add a half ounce of elderflower liqueur for a floral variation. A dash of Angostura bitters adds structure.

cocktails.name: Genovese Smash
cocktails.instructions: Place basil leaves and simple syrup in the bottom of a shaker. Muddle gently — press lightly to bruise and release the aromatic oils. Do not pulverize. Add lime juice, gin, and plenty of ice. Shake hard for 12-15 seconds until the tin is completely frosted. Double strain through a Hawthorne strainer and a fine mesh strainer into a chilled coupe or martini glass. This removes all green flecks and ice shards, leaving a clean, velvety, jade-green liquid. Garnish: slap a single large Genovese basil leaf on the back of your hand to express the oils, then float it on top of the drink.
cocktails.notes: Genovese basil specifically — it has a sweeter, more floral character than common sweet basil, with less of the anise note. The lime creates a sharper, brighter acidity than the classic lemon version, so a 2:1 rich simple syrup softens it without adding sweetness. Gentle muddling is non-negotiable. The slapped basil float garnish is essential — it perfumes every sip. This drink is often called a Basil Gin Martini because of the glass — a naming habit that dates to the 1990s cocktail boom, when anything served in a V-shaped glass got called a martini regardless of its ingredients. A true Martini is spirit plus vermouth, stirred, spirit-forward. This drink is spirit, citrus, and sweetener, shaken — a Smash. The glass is presentation. The family is everything.
cocktails.lore: A lime-forward riff on Jorg Meyer 2008 Gin Basil Smash, substituting lime for lemon and Genovese basil for common sweet basil. The shift from lemon to lime gives the drink a sharper, more tropical edge — brighter on the nose, more assertive on the finish. Often called a Basil Gin Martini because it is served in a coupe or martini glass, but the Smash is what it is and what it has always been. The glass is presentation. The template is everything.
cocktails.riffs: Use lemon instead of lime and you are making Jorg Meyer original Gin Basil Smash. Try Thai basil for an anise-forward variation. Muddle a single strawberry with the basil for a summer riff.

cocktails.name: Gimlet
cocktails.instructions: Combine gin, lime juice, and simple syrup in a shaker with ice. Shake hard for 15 seconds. Double strain into a chilled coupe or Nick & Nora glass. Garnish with a lime wheel or cucumber ribbon.
cocktails.notes: The classic recipe calls for Rose's lime cordial, but fresh lime juice with simple syrup is vastly superior. A cucumber ribbon or sprig of dill adds a beautiful botanical lift.
cocktails.lore: The Gimlet has Royal Navy origins, created in the 19th century when Surgeon General Sir Thomas Gimlette began mixing gin with lime juice to help sailors take their daily anti-scurvy ration. It appears in Raymond Chandler's The Long Goodbye, where Philip Marlowe declares that 'a real gimlet is half gin and half Rose's lime juice and nothing else.' Most modern bartenders respectfully disagree.
cocktails.riffs: Rose Gimlet: add a barspoon of rose water. Mezcal Gimlet: substitute mezcal for gin for a smoky variation.

cocktails.name: Gin & Tonic
cocktails.instructions: Fill a highball glass with ice. Add gin. Top with tonic water and a squeeze of lime. Stir gently once. Garnish with a lime wheel or wedge.
cocktails.notes: The gin-to-tonic ratio matters — 1:2 is standard but 1:3 is more refreshing on a hot day. Premium tonic waters (Fever-Tree, 1724, East Imperial) make an enormous difference. Experiment with garnishes — cucumber, rosemary, or pink pepper complement different gin styles beautifully.
cocktails.lore: The Gin & Tonic was born of British colonial necessity. Officers of the East India Company mixed their daily anti-malarial quinine tonic with gin to make it palatable. The quinine content of modern tonic water is far too low to prevent malaria but the combination endures as one of the world's most popular drinks. Spain has elevated it to an art form — the Copa de Balon glass packed with botanicals and garnishes is a Spanish contribution to cocktail culture.
cocktails.riffs: Experiment with flavored tonics — elderflower, Mediterranean, or Indian tonic water all produce distinctly different drinks with the same gin.

cocktails.name: Gin Basil Smash
cocktails.instructions: Place basil leaves and simple syrup in the bottom of a shaker. Muddle gently — bruise the leaves to release their oils, do not pulverize. Add lemon juice, gin, and ice. Shake hard for 12-15 seconds until the tin is completely frosted. Double strain through a Hawthorne and fine mesh strainer into a chilled rocks glass over ice, or serve up in a coupe. Garnish with a fresh basil leaf.
cocktails.notes: Gentle muddling is everything — overworked basil turns bitter and dark. Bruise, do not destroy. Double straining produces a cleaner, brighter green drink. A London Dry gin is the classic choice; a botanical gin with herbal notes also works beautifully.
cocktails.lore: Created by German bartender Jorg Meyer at Le Lion — Bar de Paris in Hamburg in 2008. Meyer spent an afternoon experimenting with a bunch of basil and a bottle of gin and produced one of the most important cocktails of the modern era. The Gin Basil Smash single-handedly rehabilitated the Smash template, launched a thousand herb-forward riffs, and proved that a great cocktail can come from anywhere — including a quiet afternoon in a Hamburg bar. It is now considered a modern classic and is one of the most influential drinks of the craft cocktail revival. Search Jorg Meyer to find more of his recipes.
cocktails.riffs: Genovese Smash: substitute fresh lime juice for lemon, use Genovese basil specifically, serve up in a coupe or martini glass with a slapped basil leaf float. The lime gives a sharper, more tropical acidity — balance with a slightly richer syrup.

cocktails.name: Grapefruit-Rosemary Spritzer
cocktails.instructions: Fill a chilled Collins glass halfway with ice. Add grapefruit juice and rosemary herb syrup and stir with a bar spoon to combine. Add seltzer and gently lift the grapefruit mixture from the bottom of the glass to the top to combine. Top with additional ice. Pinch the grapefruit peel over the drink to express the oils, rub the peel around the outer rim of the glass, then use it as garnish.
cocktails.notes: The ✨ next to the syrup means the recipe lives in the Craft section. Fresh grapefruit is preferred — yellow, pink, or red all work, each with a slightly different profile. The rosemary syrup is doing specific structural work here: it tempers the tartness and adds a savory piney backbone that makes the drink feel like more than juice with bubbles. ATK's headnote gives you the spirit path: add 1 oz of blanco tequila, vodka, or London dry gin to turn it into a proper spritz.
cocktails.lore: Created by Lawman Johnson and published in Cook's Illustrated (January/February 2021), then included in How to Cocktail and Cocktails Illustrated by America's Test Kitchen. 4.5 stars across 38 ratings. Johnson describes it as simple but sophisticated and not-too-sweet — which is exactly right. The rosemary syrup is the move: it adds a savory, herbal dimension that grapefruit juice alone cannot produce, and it is what separates this from every other grapefruit soda on the table.
cocktails.riffs: Add 1 oz blanco tequila for a Paloma-adjacent spritz. Add 1 oz London dry gin for something closer to a Gin & Tonic riff. Substitute thyme syrup and orange juice for a warmer, more autumnal variation.

cocktails.name: Guardian Angel
cocktails.instructions: Muddle cucumber slices in the base of a shaker. Add all remaining ingredients and ice. Shake vigorously. Double strain through a Hawthorne and fine mesh strainer into a chilled coupe. Garnish with a cucumber slice wrapped inside the rim of the glass.
cocktails.notes: Wray and Nephew is specified — the overproof funk is structural to the drink, not optional. Amaro Montenegro is the right amaro here; it is lighter and more floral than many amari, which allows the rosewater and cucumber to come through. Rosewater is measured in drops — 3 is the sweet spot, more and it dominates. Double straining produces a clean, elegant drink.
cocktails.lore: Created by Erick Castro for an Amaro Montenegro showcase event — a brief meant to highlight the Italian amaro in a cocktail context. Castro reached for Jamaican overproof rum for funk and depth, orgeat and lime for the sour backbone, and rosewater for a subtle floral lift. The combination is a deliberate nod to the classic Infante cocktail, which shares the orgeat-lime-rosewater structure, but Amaro Montenegro as the base gives it a significantly more complex, herbal character. The Educated Barfly featured it on their YouTube channel in 2020, calling it a crazy delicious drink that looks wrong on paper and right in the glass. Castro is a San Diego bartender and hospitality industry advocate who opened Raised by Wolves and Polite Provisions, two of the most celebrated bars on the West Coast.
cocktails.riffs: Try Campari in place of Amaro Montenegro for a more bitter, less floral result.

cocktails.name: Guava Mojito
cocktails.instructions: Add mint leaves and simple syrup to the bottom of a tall glass and muddle gently to release the oils. Add the rum, guava puree, and lime juice. Fill with ice and stir well. Top with club soda. Garnish with a mint sprig and lime wheel.
cocktails.notes: Guava puree gives a richer, more tropical result than guava nectar. Muddle with a light hand — over-muddled mint turns bitter. Stir rather than shake to preserve the carbonation.
cocktails.lore: From the mojito menu at Mojitos Bistro, a Cuban-American restaurant — the classic template with guava added. A variation rather than a riff: the spirit, structure, and family are unchanged, but the guava brings a gentle tropical floral quality that a classic Mojito does not have. Guava in a mojito is exactly as good as it sounds.
cocktails.riffs: The full Mojitos Bistro mojito menu is a masterclass in variations on a theme: Mango Mojito — golden and tropical, slightly sweet. Strawberry Mojito — berry-forward and fresh. Passion Fruit Mojito — tart and bold. Coconut Mojito — made with coconut rum, mellow and indulgent. Each follows the same template with a single fruit element swapped in. The template holds every time.

cocktails.name: Guillotine
cocktails.instructions: Combine all ingredients in a mixing glass. Add ice and stir until well chilled and properly diluted. Strain into a snifter over two ice cubes. Express a lemon twist over the drink and discard — do not place it in the glass.
cocktails.notes: Use a blended Scotch rather than a single malt — the blend bridges the mezcal smoke without competing with it. Honey syrup is equal parts honey and water, warmed and stirred until combined. The banana liqueur is quarter ounce only — just enough to add a tropical warmth without announcing itself. The lemon twist express is essential and should be discarded; it perfumes the nose without adding citrus to the drink.
cocktails.lore: Created by Franky Marshall for Le Boudoir, a hidden speakeasy in Brooklyn Heights entered through a fake bookshelf inside the French bistro Chez Moi. The bar is designed as a replica of Marie Antoinette chamber at Versailles — gilded mirrors, red velvet banquettes, antique sconces, and a Marie Antoinette bust that serves as a beer tap. Every cocktail on the menu is named for someone in the queen story. Marshall, whose resume includes Monkey Bar and The Dead Rabbit, developed the Guillotine specifically for the space. It became the bestseller. One guest described it as a most elegant kick in the face — which remains the most accurate tasting note in this collection. Mezcal and Scotch is a split-base that should not work and absolutely does. The recipe instructions conclude: Keep your head attached.
cocktails.riffs: Try an Islay Scotch for an aggressively smoky version. Substitute falernum for honey syrup for a more tropical, spiced result.

cocktails.name: Hibiscus Guava Agua Fresca
cocktails.instructions: Tie the hibiscus tea bag strings together and steep in room-temperature water for 45 minutes; discard bags. Stir in chilled guava nectar, mint herb syrup, and lemon juice. Refrigerate until well chilled, at least 2 hours or up to 1 day. Stir to recombine. Serve in chilled Collins glasses over ice, garnished with lemon slices and mint leaves.
cocktails.notes: Batch drink. The long room-temperature steep extracts hibiscus color and tartness without boiling bitterness. Guava gives body and tropical perfume; pineapple or mango juice can substitute.
cocktails.lore: Created by Sara Mayer for America's Test Kitchen / Cocktails Illustrated (November 2020). A highly rated zero-proof batch drink that turns agua fresca into something layered enough for cocktail service.
cocktails.riffs: Substitute pineapple or mango juice for guava nectar. For a sharper version, increase lemon slightly just before serving.

cocktails.name: Infante
cocktails.instructions: Combine all ingredients in a shaker with ice. Shake hard for 10 seconds. Strain into a rocks glass over a large ice cube. Grate fresh nutmeg over the top as garnish.
cocktails.notes: Reposado brings welcome oak and vanilla that deepens the orgeat. Blanco is brighter and more refreshing. Orange flower water is measured in drops — it perfumes the drink without dominating. Fresh nutmeg on the garnish is non-negotiable; it adds a warm, spicy finish that pulls everything together. Fortaleza and Siete Leguas are exceptional here. Liber and Co. orgeat is the obvious choice.
cocktails.lore: Created in 2009 by Giuseppe Gonzalez at Dutch Kills bar in Long Island City, New York — the bar opened by Sam Ross and Richard Boccato, two of the most important figures of the craft cocktail revival. Gonzalez replaced the Margarita orange liqueur with orgeat, a substitution that sounds simple and lands like a revelation. The almond lends body to tequila mid-palate; the orange flower water adds a perfumed warmth on the finish. Named after Pedro Infante Cruz, the beloved Mexican actor and singer who appeared in over 60 films and recorded more than 350 songs before his death in 1957. The Infante is the structural ancestor of Erick Castro Guardian Angel — swap the tequila for Amaro Montenegro and overproof rum and you have one of the most interesting cocktails of the modern era.
cocktails.riffs: Substitute rosewater for orange flower water for a more floral, delicate result — the version that inspired Erick Castro Guardian Angel. The Casper is a reposado variation with hazelnut orgeat and a rose water spritz.

cocktails.name: Irish Maid
cocktails.instructions: Add cucumber slices and simple syrup to the base of a shaker and muddle to release the juice. Add Irish whiskey, St-Germain, and lemon juice with ice. Shake vigorously until well chilled. Fine strain into a rocks glass over fresh ice. Garnish with a cucumber slice.
cocktails.notes: Use a smooth Irish whiskey — Redbreast 12 is exceptional here, Jameson is the reliable standard. Mash the cucumber, do not pulverize it — juice, not puree. The elderflower should be present but not dominant; St-Germain at 0.5 oz keeps it in its lane. Fine straining removes all cucumber pulp and gives a clean, bright drink.
cocktails.lore: The Maid family of cocktails begins with the Kentucky Maid, created by Sam Ross — the same bartender who created the Paper Plane. The Irish Maid is an adaptation credited to Jack McGarry at The Dead Rabbit in New York City, one of the most decorated cocktail bars in the world. The logic is simple: Irish whiskey, lighter and more floral than bourbon, is a natural partner for elderflower and cucumber. The result is a whiskey sour that does not taste like one — bright, garden-fresh, and deeply refreshing. It is a modern classic in the making.
cocktails.riffs: The Kentucky Maid substitutes bourbon and lime for the Irish whiskey and lemon — Sam Ross original. A Scotch Maid with a peated whisky adds a smoky counterpoint to the floral elderflower.

cocktails.name: Jungle Bird
cocktails.instructions: Combine all ingredients in a shaker with ice. Shake hard for 15 seconds. Strain over fresh ice in a tiki mug or rocks glass. Garnish with a pineapple wedge and lime wheel.
cocktails.notes: Blackstrap rum gives a richer, more molasses-forward result. The Campari is the secret ingredient — it adds bitterness that cuts the sweetness of the pineapple beautifully. Don't reduce it.
cocktails.lore: The Jungle Bird was created in 1978 at the Aviary Bar in the Kuala Lumpur Hilton, making it one of the few tiki cocktails with a confirmed origin story outside of California. It lay dormant for decades until Jeff Berry published the recipe in 2002, after which it became a modern classic and a bartender's favorite. It is notable for being one of the only tiki drinks to use Campari — an unexpected ingredient that makes it utterly distinctive.
cocktails.riffs: Substitute aged rum for the Jamaican rum for a smoother, less funky version. Add a float of overproof rum for intensity.

cocktails.name: Kir Royale
cocktails.instructions: Pour crème de cassis into a chilled champagne flute. Top with champagne. Do not stir — the bubbles will incorporate the cassis naturally.
cocktails.notes: Use a genuinely dry champagne — the cassis provides all the sweetness needed. Crème de mûre (blackberry) or crème de framboise (raspberry) make lovely variations. A regular Kir uses still white Burgundy instead of champagne.
cocktails.lore: The Kir was created by — and named after — Canon Félix Kir, Mayor of Dijon and hero of the French Resistance, who popularized the combination of local white Burgundy and blackcurrant liqueur in the 1950s. The Royale substitutes champagne for still wine, elevating it to a celebratory drink. It is the ancestor of the modern fruit-liqueur-and-sparkling wine template — including the Bellini, the Rossini, and your own French 007.
cocktails.riffs: Kir: substitute still white wine for Champagne. Substitute Chambord for creme de cassis for a raspberry variation.

cocktails.name: Lantern Fly

ingredients.name: Jamaican pot still rum (Doctor Bird recommended)

cocktails.instructions: Combine all ingredients in a cocktail shaker with ice. Shake until well chilled. Strain into a chilled coupe. Garnish with candied ginger.
cocktails.notes: Creator's spec per Punch, January 2025. Jamaican pot still rum is not interchangeable with standard Jamaican rum or blended Caribbean rum — the funk is structural. Worthy Park, Hampden, or Doctor Bird are the appropriate choices. Amargo-Vallet has limited distribution; check specialty spirits retailers. In a pinch, Angostura bitters at 0.5 oz plus 0.25 oz Campari approximates the botanical character at some cost to the amaro's depth and sweetness contribution — adjust the ginger juice accordingly.
cocktails.lore:
Jojo Colona created the Lantern Fly at Attaboy's New York location, working with two ingredients that are unusual choices within the Bug family and that produce, together, the most distinctly funky drink in the series.

Jamaican pot still rum is not a background ingredient. Made in traditional pot stills rather than the continuous column stills that produce lighter Caribbean rums, pot still Jamaican rum carries an intense, funky, almost overripe fruit quality — esters and congeners that make themselves known in any drink they inhabit. Doctor Bird, the rum Punch specifies for this recipe, is a Worthy Park expression named for the Jamaican national bird, made entirely from pot still distillate. It is not a subtle rum.

Amargo-Vallet is equally specific. The Mexican digestif amaro, made since 1881 in Mexico City and named for its French founder Adolphe Vallet, is built on a base of angostura bark — making it a relative of Angostura bitters in botanical character, with the flavor profile of a bitter liqueur rather than a concentrate. It is drier, more herbal, and less sweet than Campari, and its angostura-forward bitterness creates a different kind of tension with the ginger than Campari's more fruit-and-citrus bitterness.

The combination — funky pot still rum, angostura-forward amaro, ginger heat, lemon acid — is aggressive and layered in a way that rewards attention.
cocktails.riffs: Substitute Campari for Amargo-Vallet for a sweeter, more familiar bitter profile that tames the funk of the pot still rum rather than amplifying it. Smith & Cross, the Navy-strength Jamaican pot still rum, in place of Doctor Bird increases the proof significantly and pushes the funk further — the drink becomes considerably more demanding. Combine equal parts pot still rum and aged agricole rhum for a split-base variation with additional grassy, vegetal complexity.

cocktails.name: Large-Batch Negroni Sbagliato

ingredients.name: Orange rind, cut into long ribbons

cocktails.instructions: Fill a large punch bowl with ice. Pour in the chilled Campari, Cinzano, and Prosecco. Stir gently to combine. Garnish with long ribbons of orange rind draped across the bowl. Ladle into rocks glasses or punch cups to serve. Serves 8-10.
cocktails.notes: Everything must be well chilled before combining — this preserves the Prosecco bubbles. Do not shake. Stir once, gently. Cinzano specifically is Morgenthaler preference for this recipe. Scale down by using equal parts of each spirit: 1 oz Campari, 1 oz sweet vermouth, 1 oz Prosecco per serving.
cocktails.lore: Jeffrey Morgenthaler is known for barrel-aging cocktails and pioneering the bottled cocktail movement in the United States. But when he throws a party, he makes this. Three bottles, a punch bowl, and ice — the entire prep takes five minutes. The genius is in the equal-parts simplicity: one bottle of each, combined without measuring. Morgenthaler approach to the Sbagliato strips away any pretension and reveals what it always was — an aperitivo for a crowd, lightly bitter, endlessly refreshing, and almost impossible to mess up. Search Morgenthaler to find all three of his recipes in the collection.
cocktails.riffs: Scale to a single serving: 1 oz each Campari, sweet vermouth, Prosecco, built over ice.

cocktails.name: Last Word
cocktails.instructions: Combine all ingredients in a shaker with ice. Shake until well chilled. Fine strain into a chilled coupe. No garnish needed.
cocktails.notes: Equal parts is the law here — do not adjust the ratios. Green Chartreuse is non-negotiable; yellow Chartreuse produces a different and inferior drink. Luxardo maraschino is the standard. The equal-parts structure means the drink scales effortlessly for batching.
cocktails.lore: First appeared in print in Ted Saucier 1951 Bottoms Up, attributed to Frank Fogarty, a vaudeville comedian who performed at the Detroit Athletic Club where the drink was created during Prohibition. It spent fifty years in obscurity before Murray Stenson revived it at Zig Zag Cafe in Seattle in 2004 — an act of resurrection that launched one of the most celebrated cocktail revivals of the modern era. The Last Word is the purest expression of the equal-parts cocktail: four ingredients, each pulling identical weight, none dominating. That it works at all is a minor miracle. That it works this well is inexplicable.
cocktails.riffs: The Final Ward: substitute rye for gin and lemon for lime. The Naked and Famous: substitute mezcal for gin and Aperol for Chartreuse — a modern classic in its own right and part of this collection.

cocktails.name: Le Coucher de Soleil
cocktails.instructions: Combine gin, Cointreau, and lemon juice in a shaker with ice. Shake well and strain into an ice-filled rocks glass. Top with chilled tonic water and stir gently. Drizzle grenadine over the surface — do not stir it in. Garnish with a lemon or orange slice.
cocktails.notes: The grenadine drizzle is purely visual — it creates the sunset color gradient and should be added last, over the back of a spoon if you want it to sit on top rather than sink. Fever Tree Refreshingly Light is the recommended tonic. Moranville notes she now uses only 1 to 2 oz of tonic for a more concentrated drink — adjust to your preference. Use house-made or Liber & Co. grenadine for the best color.
cocktails.lore: Pronounced: luh coo-SHAY duh so-LAY. Encountered by food writer and cookbook author Wini Moranville on a French menu at a seaside hotel, where it was listed simply as Sunset — in English, which she found charmingly self-aware given that the French occasionally reach for English the way English speakers reach for French. Her home interpretation is a Daisy lengthened with tonic, with a grenadine drizzle added not for sweetness but for the streaks of pink and amber that mirror a setting sun over the water. Le Coucher de Soleil is her preferred name — the French rings better than the English, and she is right. Published in celebration of her cookbook Everyday French Cooking: Modern French Cuisine Made Simple.
cocktails.riffs: Reduce tonic to 1 oz for a more spirit-forward version. Substitute lime juice for lemon for a sharper edge. A splash of sparkling wine in place of tonic makes an elegant variation.

cocktails.name: Mai Tai
cocktails.instructions: Combine rum, lime juice, Cointreau, and orgeat in a shaker with ice. Shake for 15 seconds. Strain over crushed ice in a tiki mug. Garnish with a lime wheel, mint sprig, and if you have one, a cocktail umbrella.
cocktails.notes: The original uses two rums — a Jamaican aged rum and a Martinique rhum agricole. Orgeat is essential; do not substitute. Trader Vic served it with half an exhausted lime shell as garnish — a classic touch.
cocktails.lore: The Mai Tai was created by Trader Vic (Victor Bergeron) in Oakland in 1944 for friends visiting from Tahiti. One of them exclaimed 'Mai Tai — Roa Ae!' meaning 'Out of this world — the best!' in Tahitian. Trader Vic and Donn Beach (Don the Beachcomber) battled for years over who invented the tiki cocktail genre. The Mai Tai is the crown jewel of tiki culture and one of the most influential cocktails of the 20th century.
cocktails.riffs: Tia Mia: substitute Cointreau for curacao and add a split of dark rum. Adjust the orgeat ratio for a richer, more tropical result.

cocktails.name: Manhattan
cocktails.instructions: Combine whiskey, vermouth, and bitters in a mixing glass with ice. Stir for 30 seconds until well chilled. Strain into a chilled coupe or Nick & Nora glass. Garnish with a cocktail cherry.
cocktails.notes: Rye gives a spicier, drier result; bourbon gives a softer, sweeter one. Use a quality sweet vermouth — Carpano Antica is the gold standard. The cherry matters — use a Luxardo, not a maraschino.
cocktails.lore: The Manhattan was born in New York City in the 1870s, with the Manhattan Club claiming credit. It is the oldest known stirred whiskey cocktail and the direct ancestor of the Rob Roy (Scotch), the Black Manhattan (Averna), and the Toronto (Fernet). Along with the Old Fashioned and Martini it forms the holy trinity of classic American cocktails.
cocktails.riffs: Rob Roy: substitute Scotch for rye. Black Manhattan: substitute Averna amaro for sweet vermouth. Perfect Manhattan: split sweet and dry vermouth equally.

cocktails.name: Maverick
cocktails.instructions: Combine all ingredients in a cocktail shaker with ice. Shake until well chilled. Strain through a tightly gated Hawthorne strainer — or double-strain — into a chilled coupe. The mint is shaken in, not muddled; the strainer catches the leaves. Garnish with candied ginger.
cocktails.notes: Creator's spec per Punch, January 2025. A botanical gin with genuine herbal presence works better here than a neutral or citrus-forward gin — the mint needs something to harmonize with. Beefeater, Tanqueray, or Sipsmith are appropriate. The double-strain or tightly gated Hawthorne is important — mint leaf fragments in a coupe are not pleasant. Aperol's lower proof (11% ABV) means this is the lowest-alcohol drink in the Bug family; factor that in if you are building a round.
cocktails.lore:
Mike McCollum of Attaboy Nashville brought two things to the Bug family that none of the other drinks in the series have: gin as the base spirit, and fresh mint shaken directly into the cocktail.

The gin choice is interesting. The Last Word — the great-grandparent of this entire family — is a gin drink. The Paper Plane moved to bourbon. The Mosquito moved to mezcal. The Maverick returns to gin, completing a kind of circle, and pairs it with Aperol rather than Campari or Gran Classico. The result is the lightest, most herbaceous, and most approachable drink in the Bug family — Aperol's lower bitterness and higher sweetness softening the ginger's heat, gin's botanicals amplified by the mint, lemon keeping everything bright and clean.

The mint technique is the detail worth noting. Rather than muddled in the shaker or used as a garnish, the leaves are shaken whole with the other ingredients and caught by the strainer. This produces a gentler mint character than muddling — more aromatic than aggressive, woven into the drink rather than dominating it.
cocktails.riffs: Substitute Campari for Aperol for a significantly more bitter, less sweet version — closer to a gin Mosquito. Add a half ounce of green Chartreuse and reduce Aperol to 0.5 oz to push the drink back toward its Last Word ancestor. Basil shaken in place of mint produces a more savory, anise-adjacent variation worth trying.

cocktails.name: Mexico Navy
cocktails.instructions: Combine all ingredients in a shaker with ice. Shake until well chilled. Strain into a rocks glass over ice. Garnish with crystallized ginger.
cocktails.notes: The house orgeat spec at Palomar calls for equal parts Giffard orgeat and rich simple syrup (2:1) — this softens the almond intensity and gives a cleaner result. For the ginger syrup: blend 8 oz peeled fresh ginger with 1.5 cups water, strain through cheesecloth, then add equal weight of sugar and whisk until dissolved. Keeps refrigerated for up to 4 weeks. Fresh-pressed ginger syrup is dramatically better than any commercial alternative.
cocktails.lore: Created at Palomar in Portland, Oregon — a tequila riff on the Army and Navy, a gin-and-orgeat sour from the 1930s that is one of the great deep cuts of the classic cocktail canon. The substitution is elegant: tequila for gin, lime for lemon, ginger added for spice. The orgeat does the same work it does in the original — bridging the spirit and citrus with nutty sweetness — but the tequila and ginger give it an entirely different personality. The Army and Navy is British and restrained; the Mexico Navy is warm and alive.
