cocktails.riffs: The Army and Navy — the original — uses gin instead of tequila with lemon instead of lime. Both are worth knowing.

cocktails.name: Mint Julep
cocktails.instructions: Add mint leaves and simple syrup to a julep cup or rocks glass. Press the mint gently with a muddler — bruise, do not shred. Add bourbon and fill with crushed ice, packing it tightly. Stir briefly to combine. Mound more crushed ice above the rim. Garnish with a generous bouquet of fresh mint pressed close to the straw so the nose is buried in it on every sip. Serve with a short straw.
cocktails.notes: The short straw is essential — it forces the nose into the mint bouquet. Crushed ice is non-negotiable; cubed ice produces a different, inferior drink. Press the mint, do not pulverize it. A Julep cup chills beautifully and frosts on the outside, which is part of the ritual. Wheated bourbons work particularly well here.
cocktails.lore: The oldest American cocktail template still in daily production. Documented in Virginia as far back as 1803, originally made with rye or brandy before bourbon became the standard. The Kentucky Derby has served Mint Juleps since 1938 — somewhere between 120,000 and 150,000 are consumed over the two-day event, making it the single largest cocktail service operation in the world. The recipe has not changed in two centuries because it does not need to. Bourbon, mint, sugar, crushed ice. There is nothing else to say.
cocktails.riffs: The Smash is a Julep with citrus added. Rye whiskey gives a spicier, drier result. Add a float of aged rum for a Rum Julep.

cocktails.name: Mojito
cocktails.instructions: Gently muddle mint with simple syrup in the bottom of a highball glass — press, do not tear. Add lime juice, rum, and ice. Stir gently to combine. Alternatively, roll the drink before adding the soda — tip the contents back and forth between the glass and a shaker tin 4 to 5 times — then top with soda and give it a gentle stir with a straw. Rolling mixes everything evenly and distributes the mint and lime throughout the drink. Garnish with a lime wheel and mint sprig.
cocktails.notes:
Mint variety matters: use Spearmint (Mentha spicata) or Mojito Mint (Mentha x villosa), the heirloom Cuban variety. Peppermint has the wrong flavor profile entirely. Never shred the mint — gentle pressure releases the oils without releasing bitter chlorophyll.

For rum, reach for a crisp, clean white — avoid heavy, funky Jamaican rums that will clash with the delicate mint. Bottle recommendations:
• Plantation 3 Stars — a Barbados, Jamaica, and Trinidad blend, filtered clear. Subtle biscuit and sugar cane notes without crowding the palate.
• Havana Club 3 Year Old Anejo Blanco — the classic Cuban choice. Aged and charcoal-filtered, with a round, plush mouthfeel.
• Probitas Blended White Rum — a hint of classic rum character with a crisp premium backbone.
• Don Q Cristal or Bacardi Superior — excellent budget-friendly options that act as a neutral canvas for your lime and mint.
cocktails.lore: The Mojito traces its roots to 16th century Cuba. Sir Francis Drake is said to have encountered an early version on the island in the 1580s — a rough mix of aguardiente, lime, mint, and sugar called El Draque, named after him. The spirit was raw, the technique primitive, but the logic was already there. Two centuries of refinement and the arrival of proper Cuban rum turned it into something elegant. By the early 20th century La Bodeguita del Medio in Havana had made it a cultural institution. Ernest Hemingway drank there regularly, cementing the drink in literary mythology — though the record suggests he actually preferred his mojitos elsewhere and his daiquiris at La Bodeguita. Cuba being Cuba, the truth is probably more interesting than either version. It belongs to the Collins family — spirit, citrus, sweetener, mint, soda — and is one of the most ordered cocktails in the world.
cocktails.riffs: Few cocktails invite riffing as naturally as the Mojito.

cocktails.name: Moscow Mule
cocktails.instructions: Fill a copper mug with ice. Add vodka and lime juice. Top with ginger beer and gently stir to combine. Garnish with a lime wheel.
cocktails.notes: The copper mug is traditional and does keep the drink colder longer. Use a spicy, full-flavored ginger beer — Fever-Tree or Bundaberg work well. Substituting dark rum gives you a Dark & Stormy.
cocktails.lore: The Moscow Mule was invented in 1941 at the Cock 'n' Bull pub in Los Angeles as a marketing collaboration between Smirnoff vodka and a ginger beer company. Its signature copper mug was a stroke of branding genius. It represents the Highball family — spirit, mixer, ice — the simplest and most refreshing cocktail template, and the one responsible for popularizing vodka in America.
cocktails.riffs: Dark and Stormy: substitute dark rum for vodka. Kentucky Mule: substitute bourbon. Mexican Mule: substitute tequila.

cocktails.name: Mosquito
cocktails.instructions: Combine all ingredients in a cocktail shaker with ice. Shake until well chilled. Strain into a chilled coupe. Garnish with candied ginger.
cocktails.notes: Creator's spec per Punch, January 2025. The ginger juice is the heart of this drink and every drink in the Bug family — it must be made fresh. The sweetening ratio (4:3 juice to sugar by weight) is precise and intentional; adjust and the balance collapses. Campari's bitterness is what reins in the ginger's natural sweetness — they are calibrated against each other. Mezcal with genuine smoke presence is necessary; a neutral-tasting mezcal loses the tension that makes the drink interesting.
cocktails.lore:
Sam Ross created the Paper Plane in 2007 for the opening menu of Chicago's Violet Hour, drawing on the Last Word — the pre-Prohibition equal-parts classic of gin, green Chartreuse, maraschino, and lime — as his structural template. Equal parts, shaken, citrus-forward, bitter element. The Paper Plane went on to become one of the most widely traveled modern classics in the craft cocktail canon.

Ten years later, Ross revisited his own creation. At Attaboy — the celebrated bar he launched on Manhattan's Lower East Side in 2012 with partner Michael McIlroy — he assembled a new equal-parts drink called the Mosquito: mezcal, lemon, sweetened ginger juice, Campari. The architecture is the same as the Paper Plane. The personality is entirely different — smokier, spicier, more bitter, with ginger replacing Amaro Nonino's herbal sweetness and Campari sharpening the finish where Aperol had softened it.

The Mosquito became the progenitor of what Attaboy staff have dubbed the Bug Cocktail family: a growing library of equal-parts originals, now numbering more than eight, each keeping the lemon and ginger components intact while swapping the spirit and bitter element. It is, in miniature, the same creative logic that produced the Mosquito from the Paper Plane — a template passed forward, remixed, extended. Attaboy operates without written menus, relying on bartender's choice, which means these drinks exist in the bar's institutional memory as much as on any page. Publishing them is an act of preservation as much as documentation.
cocktails.riffs: The Paper Plane (Sam Ross, 2007) is the direct ancestor: bourbon, Aperol, Amaro Nonino, lemon, equal parts. The Last Word (pre-Prohibition) is the architectural grandfather: gin, green Chartreuse, maraschino, lime, equal parts. The three Bug Cocktails below are all Mosquito variations following the same equal-parts ginger-lemon template with different spirit and bitter pairings.

cocktails.name: Naked and Famous
cocktails.instructions: Combine all ingredients in a shaker with ice. Shake until well chilled. Fine strain into a chilled coupe. No garnish needed.
cocktails.notes: Equal parts is the structure — do not adjust. Yellow Chartreuse is correct here, not green; it is softer and more floral, which lets the mezcal smoke come through. Del Maguey Vida is the standard mezcal choice. The drink is more approachable than its ingredients suggest.
cocktails.lore: Created by Phil Ward at Death and Co in New York City in 2011 — a direct riff on the Last Word, with mezcal replacing gin, yellow Chartreuse replacing green, and Aperol replacing maraschino. Ward described it as his attempt to make the Last Word more approachable without sacrificing its equal-parts elegance. The swap from green to yellow Chartreuse is the key decision: it softens the herbaceous intensity and lets the mezcal smoke lead. The Naked and Famous became one of the defining modern classics almost immediately and is now a benchmark drink at craft bars worldwide.
cocktails.riffs: The Last Word is the ancestor — substitute gin, Green Chartreuse, maraschino, and lime for the original equal-parts structure.

cocktails.name: Negroni
cocktails.instructions: Combine gin, Campari, and sweet vermouth in a mixing glass with ice. Stir for 30 seconds. Strain over a large ice cube in a rocks glass. Express an orange peel over the surface and drop it in.
cocktails.notes: Equal parts is the rule — resist the urge to increase the gin. The Negroni rewards patience; stir it longer than you think necessary. Substituting bourbon for gin gives you a Boulevardier.
cocktails.lore: The Negroni was born in Florence in 1919 when Count Camillo Negroni asked bartender Fosco Scarselli to strengthen his Americano by replacing the soda water with gin. It belongs to the equal-parts family and is the gateway drug to the world of bitter, amaro-driven cocktails. The Sbagliato (with prosecco), Boulevardier (with bourbon), and Mezcal Negroni are its most celebrated variations.
cocktails.riffs: Boulevardier: substitute bourbon for gin. Mezcal Negroni: substitute mezcal for gin. Sbagliato: substitute Prosecco for gin. White Negroni: substitute Suze and Lillet Blanc.

cocktails.name: Negroni Sbagliato
cocktails.instructions: Build in a rocks glass over ice. Add Campari and sweet vermouth first, then top with Prosecco. Stir gently once — just enough to combine without losing the bubbles. Garnish with an orange slice.
cocktails.notes: Do not shake. Do not over-stir. The Prosecco is delicate and the bubbles are part of the drink. Use a good Prosecco — it is a third of the cocktail. Cava works beautifully as a slightly drier alternative.
cocktails.lore: Sbagliato means mistaken in Italian. At Bar Basso in Milan sometime in the 1970s, bartender Mirko Stocchetto was making a Negroni during a busy service and accidentally reached for a bottle of Prosecco instead of gin. Rather than discard it, he served it. The guest loved it. It became a house specialty and eventually a global classic. In 2022 a viral TikTok interview with House of the Dragon actress Olivia Cooke — in which she ordered a Negroni Sbagliato with Prosecco in a particular tone of voice — made it briefly the most Googled cocktail in the world. The happy accident has never looked back.
cocktails.riffs: The classic Negroni: substitute gin for Prosecco. Large-Batch version: equal bottles of each ingredient in a punch bowl.

cocktails.name: New Brunswick
cocktails.instructions: Combine grapefruit juice, rye, lemon juice, and simple syrup in a shaker with ice. Shake until well chilled, about 15 seconds. Strain into a highball glass filled with ice. Top with Lillet Rouge and add 2 dashes grapefruit bitters. Serve.
cocktails.notes: Ashkenazi uses Rittenhouse Rye specifically — its 100-proof backbone holds up against the assertive grapefruit without getting lost. Lillet Rouge is the house spec; substitute Carpano Antica sweet vermouth for a richer, more herbal result. Structurally this is a Sour built long — grapefruit as primary citrus, lemon as accent, served in a highball. It sits at the intersection of the Sour and Collins families, which is part of what makes it interesting.
cocktails.lore: A variation on the classic Brunswick cocktail, created by Ehren Ashkenazi of The Modern in New York City — the restaurant inside MoMA. The Brunswick template trades the Sour's usual sweetener for a fortified wine component, which adds complexity without adding sugar. Ashkenazi's use of Lillet Rouge rather than sweet vermouth gives it a lighter, more wine-forward character that suits the pink grapefruit beautifully. Published in Serious Eats.
cocktails.riffs: Substitute Campari for Lillet Rouge for a more bitter, Negroni-adjacent result. Try Aperol for a softer, lower-ABV finish.

cocktails.name: Oaxacan Old Fashioned
cocktails.instructions: Combine all ingredients in a rocks glass without ice and stir to combine. Add one large ice cube and stir again until well chilled. Express a flamed orange twist over the drink — hold a match to the skin side of the peel for a few seconds, then squeeze the oils toward the flame so they ignite briefly. Drop the singed peel into the drink.
cocktails.notes: The reposado tequila replicates the oaky, aged character of whiskey while the mezcal adds smoke and depth. Agave nectar in place of simple syrup ties the sweetener to the spirit. Many bartenders now prefer mole or chocolate bitters over Angostura — both versions are legitimate. Ward original spirit choices: El Tesoro reposado tequila and Del Maguey San Luis Del Rio single village mezcal. Both are exceptional and worth seeking out for this drink specifically.
cocktails.lore: Created by Phil Ward at Death and Co in New York City in 2007, the Oaxacan Old Fashioned is the most requested and most imitated cocktail Death and Co has ever produced — and the drink credited with opening the American cocktail world to the possibilities of mezcal. Ward replaced whiskey with a split base of reposado tequila and mezcal, and simple syrup with agave nectar. The result was something that felt entirely familiar in structure and entirely new in character. Cocktail writer Robert Simonson wrote that it opened mixologists eyes to the potential of tequila and mezcal in ways that had not been seen before. Ward went on to co-found Mayahuel, New York first dedicated mezcal and tequila bar. The Oaxacan Old Fashioned is what a truly great riff looks like — same template, transformed spirit.
cocktails.riffs: Swap Angostura for Bittermens Xocolatl Mole bitters for a smokier, more Oaxacan character. Flip the proportions — 1 oz tequila, 1 oz mezcal — for more smoke. An equal-parts split of the two spirits creates a different but equally compelling drink.

cocktails.name: Old Fashioned
cocktails.instructions: Place a large ice cube in a rocks glass. Add the bourbon, simple syrup, both bitters, and cherry juice. Stir with a cocktail mixing spoon for a full 30 seconds until well chilled and properly diluted. Express an orange peel over the glass, run it around the rim, and drop it in. Garnish with a cocktail cherry.
cocktails.notes: The 30-second stir is non-negotiable — it's what makes the texture silky. Use a good bourbon with some proof (100+) since the dilution will soften it.
cocktails.lore: The Old Fashioned is the oldest known cocktail, dating to the early 1800s — originally called simply a 'cocktail': a spirit, sugar, water, and bitters. The name came later when drinkers began requesting it 'the old-fashioned way' as bartenders started adding juices and liqueurs. It is the template from which nearly all stirred, spirit-forward cocktails descend.

cocktails.name: Paloma
cocktails.instructions: Salt the rim of a highball glass. Fill with ice. Add tequila and lime juice. Top with grapefruit juice and club soda. Stir gently. Garnish with a lime wheel.
cocktails.notes: In Mexico the Paloma is often made with Squirt or Jarritos Toronja grapefruit soda instead of fresh juice and soda — sweeter and more casual. The fresh version is vastly superior. Mezcal instead of tequila adds a beautiful smoky dimension.
cocktails.lore: The Paloma — Spanish for dove — is arguably more popular than the Margarita in Mexico itself, though far less known internationally. Its origins are murky but it became associated with Don Javier Delgado Corona, owner of La Capilla bar in Tequila, Jalisco. It belongs to the Highball family and represents the natural affinity between tequila and grapefruit — one of the great flavor pairings in cocktail making.
cocktails.riffs: Add a pinch of salt to the rim and glass for a more complex, savory version. Substitute mezcal for tequila for a smoky variation.

cocktails.name: Paper Plane
cocktails.instructions: Combine all ingredients in a shaker with ice. Shake vigorously until well chilled. Double strain into a chilled coupe.
cocktails.notes: Equal parts — easy to scale for a batch. The balance of bitter, boozy, and sour is remarkably precise. Don't substitute the Amaro Nonino — it is essential to the drink's character.
cocktails.lore: The Paper Plane was created by Sam Ross at Milk & Honey in New York City in 2007, inspired by the M.I.A. song of the same name. It is a modern classic built on the equal-parts template — four ingredients in equal measure — making it one of the easiest cocktails to remember and scale. It joins the Last Word and the Naked and Famous as the great modern equal-parts cocktails, a family that traces back to the Negroni.
cocktails.riffs: The Naked and Famous is a direct cousin — substitute mezcal for bourbon and Aperol for Campari. The equal-parts structure is the same.

cocktails.name: Pineapple Makrut Buck
cocktails.instructions: Add pineapple juice, ginger-makrut syrup, lime juice, and cream of coconut to a shaker and fill with ice. Shake until just combined and chilled, about 5 seconds — do not over-shake. Strain into a chilled highball glass half-filled with ice. Add seltzer and use a bar spoon to gently lift the juice mixture from the bottom to the top to combine. Top with additional ice and garnish with a makrut lime leaf. Serve immediately.
cocktails.notes: The ✨ next to the syrup means the recipe lives in the Craft section. The 5-second shake is deliberate — long enough to chill and combine without destroying the cream of coconut's body. Cream of coconut is not coconut cream or coconut milk: Coco Lopez or Goya are the reliable supermarket brands. If you cannot find makrut lime leaves, substitute 3 strips of lime zest and 3 strips of lemon zest. Structurally this is a zero-proof Buck — the same family as the Moscow Mule — built on pineapple and coconut rather than spirit. It drinks like a cocktail because the syrup, acid, and carbonation are doing the same structural work that spirit would do.
cocktails.lore: Created by Camila Chaparro and published in Cocktails Illustrated by America's Test Kitchen (October 2025). Five five-star reviews. This is what a genuinely good zero-proof cocktail looks like — not a juice with bubbles, but a fully considered drink where every element has a structural role. The ginger-makrut syrup, cream of coconut, and fresh lime work together the way spirit, sweetener, and acid do in a classic Buck. The result is frothy, tropical, and complex in a way that earns its place in any collection.
cocktails.riffs: Add 1–1.5 oz of white rum or coconut rum to make it a proper Buck. A float of ginger beer over the seltzer adds more heat.

cocktails.name: Pisco Sour
cocktails.instructions: Combine pisco, lime juice, simple syrup, and egg white in a shaker without ice. Dry shake vigorously for 15 seconds. Add ice and shake hard for another 15 seconds. Strain into a chilled coupe. Dot bitters on the foam and drag a toothpick through to make a decorative pattern.
cocktails.notes: The bitters pattern on the foam is traditional and visually striking — do not skip it. Peruvian pisco (Quebranta grape) gives a fuller, earthier result than Chilean pisco.
cocktails.lore: The Pisco Sour is the national cocktail of both Peru and Chile, a rivalry that has sparked genuine diplomatic tension. The Peruvian version, created by American bartender Victor Vaughen Morris in Lima in the 1920s, uses Peruvian pisco and lime. The Chilean version uses lemon. Both nations consider the other's version a heresy. It belongs to the Sour family and is one of the few classics to feature bitters as a garnish rather than a flavor component.
cocktails.riffs: Substitute gin for pisco for an egg white gin sour. Add a dash of Angostura bitters on top of the foam as aromatics.

cocktails.name: Pomegranate Spritzer
cocktails.instructions: Fill a chilled highball glass halfway with ice. Add pomegranate juice, simple syrup, and bitters; stir with a bar spoon. Add chilled seltzer and gently lift the mixture from the bottom of the glass to the top to combine. Top with additional ice. Garnish with pomegranate seeds.
cocktails.notes: Use unsweetened 100% pomegranate juice. The bitters add structure and make the drink read as a cocktail rather than juice with bubbles. Nonalcoholic old-fashioned bitters preserve zero-proof status; traditional Angostura works if trace alcohol is acceptable.
cocktails.lore: Published by America's Test Kitchen in Cocktails Illustrated (October 2025). This is a compact zero-proof spritz built around pomegranate's tart, tannic backbone rather than imitation spirits.
cocktails.riffs: Traditional Angostura bitters may be substituted if strict zero-proof status is not required. A rosemary or orange peel garnish would push it more aperitivo.

cocktails.name: Porto Flip
cocktails.instructions: Combine brandy, port, simple syrup, and egg in a shaker. Dry shake vigorously without ice for 10 seconds to emulsify the egg. Add ice and shake hard until the tin is well frosted, about 15 seconds more. Fine strain into a chilled coupe. Garnish with a generous grating of fresh nutmeg.
cocktails.notes: Fresh nutmeg on the garnish is non-negotiable — pre-ground does not have the same aromatic impact. Ruby port is the classic choice; tawny port gives a nuttier, more oxidized character. Dry shake first, then shake with ice — this sequence produces a much better foam than shaking with ice from the start.
cocktails.lore: The benchmark of the flip family and one of the oldest surviving cocktail templates. From Jerry Thomas 1887 Bartender Guide — the definitive reference of the entire cocktail canon — the Porto Flip forgoes cream entirely, letting ruby port provide its jammy, fruit-forward richness. Thomas noted that the flip produces smoothness through repeated pouring back and forth between two vessels — a technique now replaced by vigorous shaking. The port and brandy combination is one of the great flavor marriages in cocktail making.
cocktails.riffs: Substitute tawny port for a nuttier, drier result. Add a dash of Angostura bitters for complexity. A barspoon of cream makes it richer.

cocktails.name: Prado
cocktails.instructions: Combine all ingredients in a shaker without ice and dry shake vigorously to build foam. Add ice and shake again until well chilled. Double strain into a chilled coupe. Garnish with a cherry and lime wedge on a pick.
cocktails.notes: Maraschino liqueur — Luxardo is the standard, Maraska is the house recommendation at Good Neighbor. Both work; Maraska is slightly drier and more floral. The dry profile is intentional and structural — do not add simple syrup to round it out. It should be tart. The egg white bridges the tequila and lime without sweetening the drink, which is what makes it unusual. Double strain to remove any shell fragments and produce a clean foam.
cocktails.lore: First published in Stan Jones 1977 Complete Bar Guide — one of the more obscure but genuinely useful reference books of the pre-craft era. The Prado sat quietly in that book for nearly fifty years before Jesus Gomez at Good Neighbor Bar in Altadena, California started making it for a new generation of drinkers. The reception has been remarkable — likely because tequila and egg white is an unusual pairing that most people have never encountered, and the dry profile cuts against the expectation that a foamy pink drink will be sweet. It will not be. It is bright, floral, and bone dry. Published in PUNCH in 2025.
cocktails.riffs: The Infante uses orgeat instead of maraschino for a richer, nuttier profile — a close cousin worth comparing. Add a barspoon of simple syrup if you want less austerity.

cocktails.name: Praying Mantis
cocktails.instructions: Combine all ingredients in a cocktail shaker with ice. Shake until well chilled. Strain into a chilled coupe. Garnish with candied ginger.
cocktails.notes: Creator's spec per Punch, January 2025. Islay Scotch is not interchangeable with blended or Highland Scotch here — the peat is structural, not decorative. Laphroaig 10, Ardbeg 10, or Caol Ila 12 are all appropriate choices at different smoke intensities. Gran Classico is available in well-stocked craft spirits retailers; Contratto Bitter or Tempus Fugit Gran Classico are the same product. Do not substitute Campari — the bitterness profile is different enough to produce a meaningfully different drink.
cocktails.lore:
Brandon Bramhall created the Praying Mantis at Attaboy's Nashville outpost, working within the equal-parts ginger-lemon template that Sam Ross established with the Mosquito. The formula is consistent across the Bug family: a base spirit, lemon juice, sweetened ginger juice, and a bitter liqueur or amaro, all in equal proportion, all shaken and served up in a coupe. What changes is the pairing — and the pairing is everything.

Bramhall's choice of Islay Scotch and Gran Classico is the most austere and complex variation in the Bug family. Islay Scotch brings peat smoke, maritime salt, and iodine — a flavor profile that has no equivalent in any other spirit and that pairs with bitterness in ways that require careful calibration. Gran Classico, the Swiss bitter liqueur made from a nineteenth-century recipe with twenty-five herbs and roots, sits between Campari and Aperol in sweetness but carries a complexity that neither achieves. The combination produces a drink that is simultaneously more smoky, more bitter, and more herbal than the Mosquito — and considerably more demanding of the drinker.

The name is well-chosen. The praying mantis is a patient, precise, and formidable creature. So is this drink.
cocktails.riffs: Substitute blended Scotch for Islay to soften the smoke and produce a more approachable version at some cost to complexity. Campari in place of Gran Classico sharpens the bitterness and reduces the herbal depth — closer to a Scotch Mosquito than a distinct drink. For a lower-proof version, substitute a peated Scotch-style whisky liqueur (Drambuie adds honey sweetness that changes the balance significantly — account for it by reducing the ginger juice).

cocktails.name: Rabbit Szn
cocktails.instructions: Add tequila, lime juice, and ginger syrup to a shaker with a few ice cubes and whip-shake briefly — just enough to combine and chill without over-diluting. Strain into a Collins glass. Top with club soda and add ice. Float the sweet vermouth over the back of a bar spoon so it sits on top. Garnish with a mint sprig.
cocktails.notes: The whip shake is a specific technique worth understanding: use just 2-3 ice cubes instead of a full shaker of ice, and shake briefly — 3 to 5 seconds rather than the usual 12-15. The goal is to combine and slightly chill the ingredients without the full dilution of a standard shake. When you then add soda, you preserve the carbonation and get a fresher, livelier drink than if you had fully shaken and diluted first. It is the right technique for any drink that gets topped with a sparkling element. The sweet vermouth float is the signature move: it perfumes every sip from the nose and adds a layer of complexity that arrives at the end of each sip. Fell to Earth is a Philadelphia producer making exceptional vermouth; any quality sweet vermouth works. Teremana blanco is the house recommendation.
cocktails.lore: The bestselling cocktail at R&D in Philadelphia, where it has become the house crowd-pleaser. Blanco tequila, lime, ginger syrup, soda — a tequila Collins at its core — but the sweet vermouth float changes the character entirely. It arrives as a bright ginger-citrus drink and finishes with the herbal warmth of vermouth. The float technique means the first sip and the last sip are different drinks. A small and genuinely clever touch on an otherwise approachable build.
cocktails.riffs: Add a dash of Angostura bitters to the float for a more structured finish. Mezcal for half the tequila adds smokiness that plays well with the ginger.

cocktails.name: Ramble
cocktails.instructions: Short shake the gin, lemon juice, and 3/4 oz simple syrup with ice — 3 to 5 seconds only, not the usual 12-15. Strain into a double rocks glass or tall glass packed with crushed ice. In the now-empty shaker, muddle the 3 raspberries with the remaining 1/2 oz simple syrup until the syrup turns pink and the berries are fully broken down. Pour the raspberry mixture over the top of the drink. Do not stir it in — it should sit as a layer on top. Serve with a short straw so the drinker goes through the raspberry layer on every sip.
cocktails.notes: The short shake is deliberate and important. A short shake — 3 to 5 seconds rather than the full 12-15 — chills and combines the ingredients without the full dilution of a standard shake. Since the drink is served over crushed ice which will continue diluting, a lighter shake keeps the flavors cleaner and more concentrated. The raspberry layer on top is the signature: it perfumes every sip from the nose and bleeds slowly into the drink as you work through it. Plymouth gin is specified for its softer, more rounded botanical profile — a more aggressive London Dry can overpower the raspberry.
cocktails.lore: Created by Phil Ward and published in Death and Co: Modern Classic Cocktails in 2014 — the book that documented the first golden era of the New York craft cocktail scene. Not to be confused with the Ramble On, a separate Death and Co cocktail by Matthew Belanger that later became the most ordered drink on their menu. At one point the most ordered cocktail at Death and Co in its own right, which at a bar of that caliber is no small thing. The Ramble is structurally a gin sour, but the technique of muddling the raspberries separately and floating them on top is what makes it its own thing. Death and Co later opened a Denver location inside the Ramble Hotel — a bar named Death and Co inside a hotel named the Ramble, serving a cocktail named the Ramble. Whether the naming was intentional or not, it is a perfect circle.
cocktails.riffs: Substitute blackberries or strawberries for a different berry variation. The whip shake technique from the Rabbit Szn is a close relative — both use minimal ice to preserve concentration in a drink topped with something else.

cocktails.name: Ramble On
cocktails.instructions:
Combine all ingredients in a shaker with ice. Shake until well chilled. Fine strain into a chilled coupe. Garnish with a grapefruit twist. 

For the raspberry syrup: combine 1 quart raspberries with 3 cups water in a saucepan, bring to a boil for 8 minutes. Allow to cool for 10 minutes, then strain through a chinois. Combine the raspberry water with equal parts superfine sugar by weight and stir until dissolved. Refrigerate for up to 2 weeks.
cocktails.notes: The double rhubarb element is the key to this drink — Zucca Rabarbaro is the sweeter, smoother of the two rhubarb amari, while Giffard Rhubarb Liqueur is lighter and more floral. Together they build a layered rhubarb character that neither could achieve alone. Clear Creek 8-year apple brandy is Belanger choice — a quality aged apple brandy makes a significant difference here. The grapefruit twist garnish lifts the nose and adds a citrus note that the drink does not otherwise contain.
cocktails.lore: Created by Matthew Belanger at Death and Co in New York — the most ordered cocktail on their menu, a status that means something at one of the most important craft cocktail bars in the world. Named after the Led Zeppelin song. Reposado tequila and apple brandy find common ground in the wood aging both undergo, and the raspberry and rhubarb add a tart brightness that keeps the rich base spirits from becoming heavy. Tyson Buhler, Death and Co bartender, told PUNCH that menu cocktails drive sales at Death and Co New York — and the Ramble On leads all of them.
cocktails.riffs: The Ramble — Phil Ward gin and raspberry sour from the Death and Co book — is a different drink entirely, though both use raspberry as a primary flavor element.

cocktails.name: Raspberry Lime Rickey
cocktails.instructions: Combine raspberry syrup and lime juice in a 2-cup measuring cup. For each drink, fill a 12-ounce glass with ice, add 1/4 cup raspberry-lime mixture and 3/4 cup seltzer, then gently stir. Garnish with a lime slice.
cocktails.notes: The syrup is the real craft item here. ATK's sous vide method holds fruit at 140°F / 60°C for 2–3 hours, producing a vivid raspberry syrup; frozen raspberries yield especially vibrant color.
cocktails.lore: Published by America's Test Kitchen in Sous Vide for Everybody (June 2018). This is a zero-proof Rickey that keeps the template's crisp lime-and-bubbles structure while using raspberry syrup for color, aroma, and seasonal fruit depth.
cocktails.riffs: Use club soda for a sharper mineral profile or seltzer for a cleaner fruit-forward version. The raspberry-lime mixture can be batched ahead and topped with bubbles to order.

cocktails.name: Rattlesnake
cocktails.instructions: Add all ingredients to a shaker and dry shake without ice. Add ice and shake again until chilled. Fine strain into a coupe glass. Garnish with an Angostura bitters swirl.
cocktails.notes: Garnish: Angostura bitters swirl.
cocktails.lore: Created by Natasha David in New York City. David herself admits she is not a huge fan of egg whites or absinthe — yet finds the Rattlesnake unexpectedly balanced. As she puts it: ingredients in the right proportions create harmony, even if they are not always up your alley. A frothy, absinthe-spiked Whiskey Sour that earns its name.
cocktails.riffs: Omit the absinthe rinse for a more straightforward whiskey sour. The Corpse Reviver No. 2 shares the absinthe rinse technique.

cocktails.name: Rob Roy
cocktails.instructions: Combine Scotch, vermouth, and bitters in a mixing glass with ice. Stir for 30 seconds. Strain into a chilled coupe or Nick & Nora glass. Garnish with a cocktail cherry.
cocktails.notes: The Scotch you choose defines the drink entirely. A blended Scotch gives a smooth, approachable result; an Islay single malt makes it smoky and dramatic. Dry vermouth instead of sweet gives you a Dry Rob Roy.
cocktails.lore: The Rob Roy is simply a Manhattan made with Scotch whisky instead of rye or bourbon, created at the Waldorf Astoria in New York in 1894 to celebrate the opening of a Broadway operetta about the Scottish folk hero Rob Roy MacGregor. It demonstrates how the Manhattan template — whiskey, sweet vermouth, bitters — translates beautifully across different whisky styles.
cocktails.riffs: Perfect Rob Roy: split sweet and dry vermouth equally. Dry Rob Roy: use dry vermouth only.

cocktails.name: Rosemary Fizz
cocktails.instructions: Add strawberries and one and a half rosemary sprigs to a shaker with simple syrup and muddle. Add egg white, vodka, and lemon juice. Dry shake without ice for at least 15 seconds to build the foam. Add ice and St-Germain and shake again for 15 more seconds. Double strain into a coupe or rocks glass over fresh ice. Top with Prosecco. Garnish with a rosemary sprig.
cocktails.notes: The St-Germain is added with the ice in the second shake rather than the first — a deliberate choice to protect its delicate floral aromatics from the aggressive friction of the dry shake. It is a small detail that makes a difference. Dry shake for the full 15 seconds; the foam needs the time. Two small strawberries rather than one large one gives better muddling coverage.
cocktails.lore: Created by Damon Williams at Baytowne Provisions in South Walton, Florida — a beachside bar on the Gulf Coast that is not famous and does not need to be. The lineage is what matters here: an egg white sour with elderflower and a sparkling wine top, muddled rosemary and strawberry as the aromatic foundation. The thread runs from the classic Fizz template through the St-Germain era of modern American craft bartending all the way to a bar on the Emerald Coast. Every cocktail has a lineage. This one traces from Paris to New York to the Florida Panhandle, and it is a very good drink.
cocktails.riffs: Substitute gin for vodka for a more botanical result that leans into the rosemary and elderflower. Omit the Prosecco and serve straight up as a Royale variation. Blackberries in place of strawberries for an autumn version.

cocktails.name: Rosemary Gin Smash
cocktails.instructions: Muddle the rosemary sprig in the glass to release its oils — press gently, do not strip the leaves. Add gin, lemon juice, and simple syrup. Fill with ice and stir to combine. Garnish with a lemon slice and a fresh rosemary sprig.
cocktails.notes: Built in the glass with no shaking — try it as written first for comparison, then try shaking for more dilution and a colder result. The Great Eight Gin is an Austrian craft dry gin from the Peter Affenzeller distillery in Upper Austria. Any quality dry gin with botanical character works well here.
cocktails.lore: The Smash is one of cocktailing oldest templates — spirit, herb, sugar, and seasonal fruit, dating to at least 1862. The modern gin-and-herb interpretation was pioneered by German bartender Jorg Meyer, whose Gin Basil Smash (created in 2008 at Le Lion in Hamburg) inspired a generation of herb-forward riffs. This rosemary version follows that lineage: clean, aromatic, and deeply refreshing. Found on a German cocktail website featuring The Great Eight Gin, an Austrian craft dry gin from the Peter Affenzeller distillery.
cocktails.riffs: The direct ancestor of this drink is the Gin Basil Smash, created by German bartender Jorg Meyer at Le Lion in Hamburg in 2008 — same template, basil instead of rosemary. Worth making both back to back.

cocktails.name: Sicilian Sojourn
cocktails.instructions: Add tarragon leaves and simple syrup to the base of a cocktail shaker and muddle until fragrant, about 30 seconds. Add blood orange juice and lemon juice, then fill shaker with ice. Shake until just combined and chilled, about 5 seconds — do not over-shake. Double-strain into a chilled Collins glass half-filled with ice. Add seltzer and use a bar spoon to gently lift the juice mixture from the bottom of the glass to the top to combine. Top with additional ice and garnish with a tarragon sprig. Serve immediately.
cocktails.notes: Double-straining is essential here — it removes all tarragon leaf fragments and produces the clean, jewel-bright magenta color that makes this drink as beautiful as it tastes. The 5-second shake is deliberate; longer dilutes the vivid color and softens the tarragon. Blood oranges are a winter fruit — peak season is December through March. Out of season, navel oranges work but the color and raspberry-bitter complexity of the blood orange won't be there. Fresh basil is a documented substitute for tarragon if you prefer a sweeter, more floral herbal note.
cocktails.lore: Created by Camila Chaparro and published in How to Cocktail and Cocktails Illustrated by America's Test Kitchen (November 2020). 4.5 stars across 14 ratings. Blood oranges originated in the southern Mediterranean and feature prominently in Sicilian cuisine — the name earns itself. The tarragon is the move: its anise-licorice quality forms a classic Mediterranean pairing with citrus that turns a beautiful juice into something genuinely complex. This is zero-proof cocktail making at its most considered.
cocktails.riffs: Add 1 oz of Aperol for a low-ABV spritz with complementary bitter orange notes. Add 1 oz of gin for a more botanical, spirit-forward build. Substitute fresh basil for tarragon for a sweeter, less anise-forward variation.

cocktails.name: Sidecar
cocktails.instructions: Sugar the rim of a coupe glass. Combine cognac, Cointreau, and lemon juice in a shaker with ice. Shake hard for 15 seconds. Double strain into the prepared glass.
cocktails.notes: The sugared rim is traditional but optional — omit it if you prefer a drier drink. The ratio of spirit to orange liqueur to citrus (2:1:1 or 8:3:3) is the same template as the Margarita and Cosmopolitan.
cocktails.lore: The Sidecar was born in Paris around World War I, with Harry's New York Bar and the Ritz both claiming credit. It is one of the great classic Daisies — the same family as the Margarita and Cosmopolitan — and essentially a Cognac sour with orange liqueur substituting for simple syrup. Its name supposedly comes from the motorcycle sidecar in which a regular patron arrived.
cocktails.riffs: Brandy Crusta: add maraschino and bitters, add a sugar-rimmed crusta — the ancestor of this drink. Substitute Calvados for cognac for a French apple variation.

cocktails.name: Singapore Sling
cocktails.instructions: Combine all ingredients in a shaker with ice. Shake well. Strain into a Collins glass filled with fresh ice. Garnish with a pineapple slice and a maraschino cherry.
cocktails.notes: Cherry Heering specifically — not generic cherry brandy. The Benedictine is the secret weapon and should not be omitted; it adds a herbal depth that is hard to identify but impossible to miss when absent. Fresh pineapple juice makes a significant difference over canned. The grenadine provides color as much as sweetness — housemade grenadine gives a far better result than commercial.
cocktails.lore:
Created sometime between 1899 and 1915 by Ngiam Tong Boon, a Hainanese-Chinese bartender at the Long Bar in Raffles Hotel, Singapore. The original recipe was never formally recorded — the closest thing to a primary source is a recipe hastily scrawled on a bar chit in 1936 by a visitor who thought to ask a waiter how it was made.

The drink was conceived as a workaround. In colonial Singapore, women were not permitted to consume alcohol in public — but fruit juice was perfectly acceptable. The Singapore Sling's pink color and tropical sweetness gave women plausible deniability, a cocktail disguised as something respectable. Ngiam Tong Boon built the subversion right into the recipe.

The Long Bar where it was born did not survive the war intact. Japanese forces occupied Raffles in 1942, using it as a prisoner of war transit camp, and whatever records existed were lost. The version served today is reconstructed from the memories of former bartenders and that lone 1936 chit.

The hotel was later restored to its colonial-era splendor, and the Long Bar now serves thousands of Singapore Slings a day — guests still encouraged, as they always were, to throw their peanut shells on the floor.
cocktails.riffs: Reduce grenadine and pineapple for a drier, more spirit-forward version. Add a float of dark rum for a richer tropical character.

cocktails.name: Six Seeds
cocktails.instructions: Add gin, grapefruit juice, lemon juice, grenadine, bitters, and orange peels to a shaker with ice. Shake until well chilled. Fine strain into a chilled coupe. Top with sparkling wine. Garnish with freshly grated cinnamon.
cocktails.notes: House-made grenadine is specified and matters here — the pomegranate is the center of the drink, and store-bought grenadine is not grenadine. Morgenthaler's grenadine spec is in the Craft library. Suntory Roku is the house gin — its yuzu and sakura petal botanicals add a subtle floral quality that amplifies the pomegranate. The orange peels go into the shaker, not just expressed over the top; shaking with them extracts oil into the body of the drink. The cinnamon garnish should be freshly grated over the surface just before serving.
cocktails.lore: Created by Ali Martin at The Up and Up in Greenwich Village in 2019. Named for the six pomegranate seeds Persephone ate in the underworld, binding herself to Hades and causing Demeter to withdraw the harvest from the earth — the mythological origin of winter. Martin set out to create a drink worthy of a wedding toast for Persephone and Hades: the pomegranate at center stage, a touch of bubbles for the occasion, and cinnamon warmth at the finish, just enough to make the underworld feel inviting. Everyone knows the best parties happen in December.
cocktails.riffs: Substitute Campari for grenadine for a more bitter, Negroni-adjacent variation. Add a barspoon of St-Germain for a more floral result.

cocktails.name: Sonambula
cocktails.instructions:
Shake all ingredients with ice. Strain into a chilled coupe. Garnish with a lemon wheel.

Jalapeno infusion: Slice 3 jalapenos per liter of blanco tequila. Steep for 10-20 minutes, tasting regularly, then strain. Adjust time for heat preference.

Chamomile syrup: Make a strong chamomile tea, then combine 2 parts sugar to 1 part hot tea and stir to dissolve. Cool before using.
cocktails.notes: The Xocolatl Mole bitters are essential — they draw out depth in the tequila and bridge the floral chamomile with the heat of the jalapeno. Do not skip them or substitute. Time your jalapeno infusion carefully — 10 minutes gives gentle warmth, 20 gives serious heat.
cocktails.lore: First developed when Ivy Mix was working at Fort Defiance in Brooklyn, the Sonambula followed her to Clover Club and ultimately became a permanent fixture on the menu at Leyenda — her pan-Latin cocktail bar on Smith Street in Brooklyn. The name means sleepwalker in Spanish, and the drink lives up to it: the jalapeno heat creeps in quietly, the chamomile soothes, and the mole bitters add a layer of complexity that makes you keep reaching for the glass. Mix is one of the defining figures of the craft cocktail revolution — co-founder of Speed Rack, a global all-femme bartending competition that has raised millions for breast cancer research, and author of Spirits of Latin America. | Search Ivy Mix to find more of her recipes.
cocktails.riffs: Add a barspoon of elderflower liqueur for a more floral variation.

cocktails.name: Southside
cocktails.instructions: Gently muddle mint with simple syrup in the bottom of a shaker tin — press, do not tear. Add gin, lime juice, and ice. Shake hard for 15 seconds. Double strain through a fine mesh strainer into a chilled coupe. Garnish with a lime wheel and mint sprig.
cocktails.notes: Double strain through a fine mesh sieve to remove all mint fragments. The key is bruising the mint gently — over-muddling releases bitter chlorophyll from the stems.
cocktails.lore: The Southside is a gin sour with fresh mint — essentially a gin Mojito served up. Its origins are disputed between the 21 Club in New York and the South Side of Chicago during Prohibition, where bootleggers allegedly used mint and citrus to mask the taste of rough spirits. It remains a fixture of country club and yacht club culture, particularly in the American Northeast.
cocktails.riffs: Southside Fizz: top with soda water and serve tall over ice.

cocktails.name: Springs First Bloom
cocktails.instructions: Combine all ingredients in a shaker and dry shake vigorously without ice to build the foam. Add ice and shake again until well chilled. Double strain through a fine mesh strainer into a chilled coupe. Garnish with a single mint leaf or microgreen.
cocktails.notes: Hendricks is specified and should not be substituted — its cucumber and botanical notes are structural to the drink, not incidental. The lemongrass syrup takes time but is worth making; it also works beautifully in a Daiquiri or Gimlet. Lavender bitters are essential — Fee Brothers and Scrappy both make excellent versions. The microgreen garnish is elegant and intentional.
cocktails.lore: Created by Charlotte Voisey, one of the most decorated bartenders of the modern era — William Grant and Sons brand ambassador, Tales of the Cocktail Foundation board member, and a driving force in bringing craft bartending into the mainstream consciousness. Spring First Bloom is a showcase for what a thoughtfully constructed Egg White Sour can be: Hendricks cucumber botanicals, St-Germain elderflower, lemongrass, lavender bitters, and egg white foam, all working in concert. Published in Liquor.com. The name is apt — this is what spring tastes like.
cocktails.riffs: The lemongrass syrup works in almost any floral sour. Try it in a Gimlet or a Bees Knees riff.

cocktails.name: Strawberry Caipirinha
cocktails.instructions: Remove the white pith from the lime half and cut into 4 wedges. Add to a rocks glass with the strawberries and sugar. Muddle firmly until the strawberries are fully broken down and the lime has released its juice. Add cachaca and fill with crushed or regular ice. Stir well. Garnish with a fresh strawberry on the rim.
cocktails.notes: Use ripe, in-season strawberries — underripe strawberries are mostly water and will produce a flat, pink drink rather than a vibrant one. Taste before adding more sugar as ripe strawberries bring their own sweetness. Crushed ice gives a better result than cubed here.
cocktails.lore: The Strawberry Caipirinha is the most popular variation of Brazil national cocktail — and the one most likely to convert someone who thinks they do not like cachaca. The fruit softens the spirit forward edge of the classic while the lime keeps the brightness. It follows the same logic as the classic: muddle, spirit, ice. The template is unchanged. Only the fruit has moved.
cocktails.riffs: Add a few fresh basil leaves to the muddle for an herbal variation. A splash of fresh orange juice adds brightness. For a sparkling version, top with a splash of soda water.

cocktails.name: Thou Shall Not Be Named
cocktails.instructions: Combine all ingredients in a mixing glass with ice. Stir until well chilled and properly diluted. Strain into a rocks glass over a large ice cube. Garnish with an expressed lemon twist.
cocktails.notes: Amaro Sfumato Rabarbaro is the key ingredient — a smoky rhubarb-root amaro from Cappelletti that is dark, bitter, and deeply complex. It pulls out the bitter orange notes from the Torino vermouth while the mezcal adds a layer of smoke. El Tesoro reposado and Del Maguey Vida mezcal are the original choices but any quality equivalents work. Stir, do not shake — this is a stirred spirit-forward drink.
cocktails.lore: Created by Alicia Perry at Polite Provisions in San Diego — the James Beard-nominated bar owned by Erick Castro, who is already in this collection via the Guardian Angel. Perry describes the drink simply as stirred and direct, which is exactly right. Working from the Boulevardier framework, she swaps whiskey for a reposado-mezcal split and replaces Campari with Amaro Sfumato Rabarbaro, a smoky rhubarb amaro that changes the character of the drink entirely. It retains the Negroni family structure while going somewhere whiskey could never take it. First published in PUNCH in 2022.
cocktails.riffs: Substitute Campari for the Sfumato for a more approachable but less distinctive version. A full ounce of mezcal makes it significantly smokier.

cocktails.name: Three Dots and a Dash
cocktails.instructions: For the vanilla honey syrup: dissolve honey in an equal volume of warm water and add a drop of vanilla extract. Combine all ingredients in a shaker with crushed or pebble ice and 3-4 ice cubes. Shake until well chilled and frosty. Pour unstrained into a tiki mug or tall glass — the ice goes in with the drink. Garnish with a pineapple leaf, three cocktail cherries on a pick, and a pineapple spear or wedge. The orchid is optional but encouraged.
cocktails.notes: Use a dry curacao rather than a sweet triple sec — the distinction matters here. Rhum agricole and Jamaican rum together give the drink both the grassy brightness of cane juice rum and the funky depth of molasses rum. The unstrained pour is deliberate — the dilution and texture from the crushed ice is part of the drink. Three cherries on the garnish is not decoration; the name is Morse code for V, the victory symbol. This spec by Dushan Zaric omits the orange juice of the original Donn Beach recipe, which the modern craft tiki world has largely endorsed.
cocktails.lore: Created by Donn Beach — born Ernest Raymond Beaumont Gantt — at Don the Beachcomber in Hollywood in the 1940s. The name is Morse code for the letter V, the victory sign, and was created as a celebration of the Allied victory in World War II. Three dots and a dash — dot dot dot dash — the most famous letter in the history of radio transmission. The version in this collection was developed by Dushan Zaric, the cocktail architect behind Employees Only and Macao Trading Co in New York City, for the relaunch of one of Southern California oldest tiki bars. Zaric removed the orange juice of the original, tightening the spec and pushing the rum and spice elements forward. Donn Beach invented tiki. This drink is why.
cocktails.riffs: The original Donn Beach recipe includes 1 oz orange juice — add it back for a rounder, less spirit-forward version. A float of overproof Jamaican rum adds intensity.

cocktails.name: Tia Mia
cocktails.instructions: Combine all ingredients and shake with ice. Strain into a double rocks glass filled with crushed ice. Garnish with a lime wheel, mint sprig, and an orchid if you have one.
cocktails.notes: The name is a play on Mai Tai — swap the letters. Tia Mia is also Spanish for my aunt, the name Mix gave to a regular she knew in Guatemala. Use a smoky, expressive mezcal — Del Maguey Vida is the classic choice. Jamaican rum brings funk and depth; any full-bodied aged Jamaican rum works. Crushed ice is part of the identity.
cocktails.lore: In the mid-2000s, Ivy Mix had a habit of floating a splash of mezcal on cocktails she liked — including the Mai Tai. Around 2010, working at Lani Kai in New York, she committed to a full ounce and the Tia Mia was born. A mezcal-and-Jamaican-rum riff on Trader Vic 1944 original, it quickly earned a following among New York bartenders and drinkers and is now considered a modern tropical classic. Mix went on to co-found Leyenda in Brooklyn, a pan-Latin cocktail bar ranked among the world best, and to write Spirits of Latin America — a book that treats Latin spirits as cultural history, travel, and place, not just bottles on a backbar. | Search Ivy Mix to find more of her recipes.
cocktails.riffs: The Mai Tai is the direct ancestor — substitute curacao for orgeat and lime for the base.

cocktails.name: Tom Collins
cocktails.instructions: Combine gin, lemon juice, and simple syrup in a shaker with ice. Shake for 10 seconds. Strain into a Collins glass over fresh ice. Top with club soda. Stir gently. Garnish with a lemon wheel and cocktail cherry.
cocktails.notes: Don't over-shake — you are about to add carbonation. Strain over fresh ice to keep the dilution controlled. A John Collins substitutes bourbon for gin; a Vodka Collins uses vodka.
cocktails.lore: The Tom Collins is a gin fizz served long over ice, one of the great summer cocktails. Its name comes from an 1874 practical joke — the Tom Collins Hoax — where people would tell friends that a man named Tom Collins had been spreading rumors about them, sending them on a wild chase to find him at various bars. The drink was ready and waiting when they arrived, puzzled and thirsty. It represents the Fizz family — spirit, citrus, sweetener, soda.
cocktails.riffs: John Collins: substitute whiskey for gin. Vodka Collins: substitute vodka. Add a barspoon of elderflower liqueur for a floral Hugo Collins variation.

cocktails.name: Toreador
cocktails.instructions: Combine all ingredients in a shaker with ice. Shake until well chilled, about 15 seconds. Fine strain into a chilled coupe. Garnish with a lime wedge on the rim.
cocktails.notes: Apricot liqueur rather than apricot brandy — the liqueur is softer and more floral. Luxardo Apricot or Giffard Abricot du Roussillon are the best choices. Blanco tequila keeps the agave notes clean and forward; reposado gives a mellower, oakier result. The spec from PUNCH via Hayden Lambert at Above Board, Melbourne — considered one of the finest versions of this underappreciated classic.
cocktails.lore: First published by British bartender William Tarling in the 1937 Cafe Royal Bar Book — predating the first written Margarita recipe by several years. The Toreador and the Margarita are cousins: both are tequila Daisies, one using orange liqueur, the other apricot. The fact that orange won the popularity contest is a matter of marketing, economics, and availability rather than quality. In Australia, the Toreador commands serious respect and is a standard entry in the mental recipe book of most professional bartenders. In the United States, it remains essentially unknown. It should not be. Named for the bullfighter on horseback — as with several cocktails in Tarlings book that paid tribute to Mexico.
cocktails.riffs: The original 1937 Tarling recipe called for equal parts tequila, apricot brandy, and lime with no sweetener — sharper and more austere. Try reposado for a warmer, mellower variation.

cocktails.name: Triple Crown
cocktails.instructions: Add bourbon, pamplemousse, lemon juice, and Montenegro Amaro to a cocktail shaker. Fill two-thirds full with ice and shake until well chilled, about 15 seconds. Strain into a chilled coupe and garnish with a lemon twist.
cocktails.notes: A complex whiskey sour that rewards good ingredients. Eagle Rare single-barrel bourbon brings depth and vanilla backbone. Combier's Pamplemousse Rose is the preferred pamplemousse — the citrusy grapefruit richness ties the Montenegro's herbal bitterness to the lemon beautifully. The equal three-quarter measure of pamplemousse, lemon, and amaro is the architecture of the drink — don't adjust without considering what you're changing.
cocktails.lore: The Triple Crown comes from Jay Zimmerman of ba'sik in Williamsburg, Brooklyn, and was featured in Brooklyn Bartender by Carey Jones. The name earns its place three times over: three equal parts anchor the recipe; bourbon is the sport of Kentucky and horse racing royalty; and the combination of pamplemousse, lemon, and Montenegro Amaro represents a hat trick of complexity that takes a classic whiskey sour template and transforms it into something more layered and surprising. It is, as Jones writes, a complex whiskey sour packed full of flavor.

cocktails.name: Vieux Carré
cocktails.instructions: Combine all liquid ingredients in a mixing glass with ice. Stir for 30-40 seconds. Strain over a large ice cube in a rocks glass. Garnish with an expressed lemon peel.
cocktails.notes: This is a complex, spirit-forward drink — use quality ingredients throughout. Bénédictine is the traditional herbal liqueur but any quality amaro works. The two bitters together are essential.
cocktails.lore: The Vieux Carré — French for 'Old Square,' the name for the French Quarter of New Orleans — was created by head bartender Walter Bergeron at the Hotel Monteleone in the 1930s. It is unique in combining both rye whiskey and cognac as co-base spirits, united by sweet vermouth and Bénédictine. The Hotel Monteleone's Carousel Bar, which literally rotates, remains one of the great American cocktail destinations.
cocktails.riffs: Remove the cognac and increase the rye for a more whiskey-forward variation. Add a rinse of absinthe for extra herbaceous depth.

cocktails.name: Whiskey Sour
cocktails.instructions: Dry shake all ingredients without ice for 15 seconds to emulsify the egg white. Add ice and shake hard for another 15 seconds. Strain into a rocks glass over ice. Dash bitters on the foam and drag a toothpick through for a decorative pattern.
cocktails.notes: The egg white is optional but transforms the texture — silky and luxurious. The dry shake first is essential to build the foam. For a Boston Sour, serve up in a coupe.
cocktails.lore: The Whiskey Sour dates to at least 1862, appearing in Jerry Thomas's seminal bartending guide. It represents the entire Sour family — spirit, citrus, sweetener — which is the most important template in cocktail making. The addition of egg white elevates it to a Fizz or Boston Sour. Nearly every fruit-forward modern cocktail traces its lineage to this template.
cocktails.riffs: New York Sour: float red wine on top. Boston Sour: add egg white. Add a dash of Angostura bitters for more structure.

cocktails.name: White Lady
cocktails.instructions: Dry shake all ingredients without ice to build the foam. Add ice and shake again until well chilled. Fine strain into a chilled coupe. No garnish, or a thin lemon twist if you must.
cocktails.notes: The egg white is optional but highly recommended — it gives the drink a silky texture and a beautiful white foam that explains the name. Dry shake first, then shake with ice. Cointreau specifically, not generic triple sec — the quality of the orange liqueur matters here. A good London dry gin is the right choice.
cocktails.lore: Harry Craddock created the White Lady at the American Bar at the Savoy in London in 1930, publishing it in The Savoy Cocktail Book the same year — one of the most important bartending reference books ever written. It is a Daisy in its purest form: gin, orange liqueur, citrus, served up. The egg white was Craddock addition, lifting a clean three-ingredient Sour into something more refined. The Savoy Cocktail Book codified an entire era of classic cocktail making during Prohibition, when American bartenders fled to London and brought their craft with them. The White Lady is one of its finest results.
cocktails.riffs: Omit the egg white for a sharper, more citrus-forward version. Add a dash of orange bitters for depth. Some bartenders add a barspoon of simple syrup for a rounder finish.

cocktails.name: White Russian

ingredients.name: Mr. Black Cold Brew Coffee Liqueur

cocktails.instructions: Fill a rocks glass with ice. Add vodka and coffee liqueur. Float cream on top by pouring it slowly over the back of a spoon. Stir gently before drinking, or leave it to swirl for the visual effect.
cocktails.notes: The float is visual drama — the swirling cream and coffee is part of the experience. Mr. Black is a significant upgrade over Kahlúa. For a Black Russian, simply omit the cream.
cocktails.lore: The White Russian was created in 1949 by a Belgian bartender named Gustave Tops at the Hotel Metropole in Brussels, in honor of Perle Mesta, U.S. Ambassador to Luxembourg. It languished in relative obscurity until The Big Lebowski (1998), in which Jeff Bridges's character The Dude drinks them constantly — catapulting it back into cultural relevance. 'The Dude abides.'
cocktails.riffs: Black Russian: omit the cream entirely. Substitute oat milk or coconut cream for a dairy-free variation.

cocktails.name: Wildberry Lillet Spritz
cocktails.instructions: Fill a large wine glass generously with ice. Pour in the Lillet Blanc. Top with Schweppes Wild Berry lemonade. Add the berries — halve any larger strawberries. Stir once gently and serve immediately.
cocktails.notes: Schweppes Wild Berry is the classic mixer and may require a specialty or European grocery store in the US. Thomas Henry Wild Berry is an excellent substitute. In a pinch, use a quality sparkling water with a splash of crème de cassis and a few drops of raspberry syrup. Lillet Rosé works beautifully in place of Blanc for a fruitier, more floral result.
cocktails.lore: The Wildberry Lillet is a modern German aperitivo phenomenon — simple, achingly pretty, and perfectly suited to warm evenings. It takes its name from the combination of Lillet Blanc, a French Bordeaux-based apéritif wine with notes of candied orange and citrus, and Schweppes Wild Berry lemonade, which provides the distinctive berry sparkle. While not a classic in the historical sense, it has achieved cult status in German-speaking countries and is one of the defining drinks of European summer terrace culture.
cocktails.riffs: Substitute Aperol for a more bitter aperitivo variation. Add a splash of elderflower tonic for a more aromatic result.

cocktails.name: Zuzu's Petals
cocktails.instructions: Add the quartered lime to a shaker tin and muddle firmly to release the juice. Add tequila, Demerara syrup, ginger syrup, Tabasco, and rose water. Fill with ice and shake hard. Dump the entire contents unstrained into a chilled double rocks glass. Top with additional ice if needed. No garnish. For Demerara syrup: 1 cup Demerara sugar, half cup water, simmer until dissolved, cool and bottle. Refrigerates up to 2 weeks. For fresh ginger syrup: juice three quarters lb peeled ginger root, add sugar at a ratio of one third cup sugar per half cup juice, blend on high for 2 minutes until fully dissolved. Refrigerates up to 1 week.
cocktails.notes: The rose water is 2 dashes only — it is not a flavor, it is a presence. Tabasco Habanero specifically, not the original red Tabasco; the habanero version is fruitier and its heat lands differently. Fresh ginger syrup is worth making properly — the blender method produces a cleaner, more intense result than steeping. The dump technique, pouring the whole tin unstrained into the glass, is deliberate: the muddled lime pieces stay in the drink and continue releasing as you sip.
cocktails.lore: Created by Matt Piacentini at The Up and Up in Greenwich Village, New York in 2016 — the year every guest seemed to ask the same question: do you have any spicy tequila drinks? The name comes from the scene in It is a Wonderful Life where George Bailey, returned from his supernatural journey, finds his daughter Zuzu's flower petals in his coat pocket. The petals are proof that Bedford Falls is restored and that he was never erased from it. In the cocktail, as in the film, just a few drops of rose water — petals in liquid form — transform a rustic blend of tequila, lime, ginger, and Demerara into something aromatic and ethereal. Piacentini has watched the film every year at Christmas since film school in London, and describes it as a full recharge of the gratitude meter. The cocktail became the most popular drink at The Up and Up by a significant margin. It is a celebration of the vibrance of simply being alive.
cocktails.riffs: Reduce the Tabasco to 2-3 drops for a gentler heat. Omit the rose water and you have a very good spicy tequila sour, but you lose the thing that makes it singular.
